In fact, I never heard soloing on drums, outside of Baby Dodds, doing the things he did. I never heard soloing in those days. The drummer played drums for the band. You didn't take no breaks. And here is Augie, just laying down that beat, and -- let's get it going, maybe it'll take us two hours, to hit that beautiful groove where the world could come to an end and it doesn't matter.
Right.

Because you're into it, you understand. So -- and now he's exposed on the bandstand. When the music is -- when somebody is laying out and Harvey is talking to the boys about, when you're done you don't die, because you go on. And you change bodies and -- but you go on. And these things -- maybe I believe it now, but at that time, -- for for Augie, and it was the fourth night, we just started playing. And Augie was not the kind of guy that you could talk to. He was dour, that kind of -- I mean, you would have to go in a room and take a quiet time and say, well, is this the moment I should broach the subject? You didn't know how he was going to react.

Musically, fine. He loved me, we got along real fine. But we didn't have to talk. We played. But he overheard this. And here it is, 9:00, we started and it's 10:00, he's back in his drums. And nobody wants to say anything, ______ doesn't

want to say nothing. And he packs the drums and calls a cab and hauls him out to the South Side, 1800 or somewhere, where some gangsters . . . to go to work as a bartender, which is what he did, and just put the drums down.

And we didn't find out til later what it was, that it was this conversation that was driving him up the wall. And an interesting story about this is that, years later, it was little George . . . that was in the car, and Hillard is in the front with Murphy.
No, no, with Earl Murphy.
Earl Murphy.

And myself. And George is in the back, and I don't know who he's with. But they were talking about the same subject, about having a seance and all that. Murphy says, what the hell are they talking about? I says, I don't know, they didn't give me any.
(Laughter.)
But this was Augie's . . .
You say your time with -- when he was over -- around 1931.
Around then.
And you had worked together, made the record. Was there a place called the Cellar that you worked at during that period?

Yes, My Cellar was a place and the Three Deuces was a place. And Winnie and I broke up after the El Dorado Club. We had gone out to the El Dorado Club, we were still talking, but I had met a New Orleans kid by the name of Bill Kennedy, who was a fighter. He'd been a great fighter. Fought for the championship and all that. Lost, but he'd been a great lightweight fighter.

And he loved this music. There was a fascination between us. We liked each other. And he didn't like what was happening to him. He kept telling me that Winnie was just taking me. I was paying for my musical education, is what he was saying. And of course, in the El Dorado Club after that, we were still together, but this thing was going on underneath.

And it was at the El Dorado that Winnie got into an argument with the boss. And the boss grabbed him and tore his false arm off and threw it across the floor. Arm and coat. And Winnie got up and he says, 'let's go.' We all quit to a man. It was Freeman and the whole band. Krupa -- I know Krupa and Freeman were in that band together. We played the floor show, we played everything. And it was a great experience, great band.
So it was about that time that I decided I would go live with Bill, because I didn't -- I was beginning to get fascinated with living with him. And that style, that I could
go to work. Art was working with me when we were not working.
It was controlling your life.

Controlling, very much. And Bill kind of broke us up. And I went to live with Bill. So I started drifting away. But Win (Wingy Mannone) opened that My Cellar, and he had done some . . . Had nothing for me, and I came down there to visit. And I was just fortunate that the same night I came down, Bix came down. And I just sat there and listened.

And then, finally, this spotlight, there was one spotlight, and Sam Beers was running the place. B-e-e-r-s, he was the boss then that you might run into occasionally now in Annapolis or in Europe, the understanding man that puts the music first and the cash register second. It's a rarity, a tremendous rarity. The man that loves the arts.
So he had Wingy's Winnie's band. And they spotlighted on Bix, and the whole audience was musicians. There might have been a couple of dancers that hung around.
Where was that?
That was almost directly across from 222 N. State, which puts it north of Lake Street, where Fritzel's later was.
Oh, yes.
But it's closed now, I believe.
Yeah.
But Fritzel's was there, and there was
a downstairs . State and Lake , just a little north, on the East Side. Where the Three Deuces was across the street on the West Side.

So I was this thing and . . . musician. And they got Bix to sit in. And Bix called some tune for some reason . . . . Whatever it was, Win, just got up again and walked over to me and grabbed me like everything's forgotten, sat me up there to play with them. And I will never forget it, because I played with him until the porter swept us out.
Councilman was a drummer --
Oh, Bob Councilman.
Played drums. And we just played and played and played. The only time we stopped was when Bix wanted to play a little piano. And I'm amazed, how much he played.

Now, the funny thing, my reaction then was that I liked Winnie better than Bix, in person, because Win, swung harder and he just made me feel like the music was moving. Bix, -- now that I listen to Bix, Bix had so many beautiful ideas, but it had very little to do with moving me rhythmically or anything.
Right, because he wasn't --
No, although his bands moved.
Yeah, he wasn't really like Louis,
rhythmically that interesting.

No, no, two different things. And I remember. But I stuck with him all night. The porter swept us out at 6:00 in the morning. Everybody was gone, Wingy Winnie was gone, everybody was gone. We're still playing. It was a great kick, that you could get that interested in playing music. Nothing else mattered.

Of course, the time was right. Most of us weren't married, we weren't supporting anyone, just ourselves. So music could be the most important. It was just like the kids today going to school, with an allowance. They don't have to go out there and work. Supposing they miss a meal and have to eat pretzels? It's the same thing. So the time was ripe for us to follow our involvement. Later on, the time would have been wrong, because you take on weight and you have to support a family. You can't allow yourself all these extravaganzas.

So by that time you should have arrived to some statement. So many incidents with Win.7y during that time, I'm not covering them all, I'm covering most of the highlights. But again, I can count more the times that we were out of work than we were working.

Now, one of the jobs we had was, Win.7y got the chance to put together a big band and work at the Aragon one night and the Trianon the next night, or vice versa, I forget which. But . . . King was the big band at one of the places we

were playing opposite. Now, he's got -- Wingy got Paul Margs .., besides himself, Floyd O'Brien, I remember that. Either -- I think it was .. And we had every hot musician -- what they called hot -- in that band. No music, it was all head arrangements.

I've done that since then many times, put together ten -- if you get the right people, like Eddie Johnson and Nat Jones, and they set those riffs, you really don't need it. All you have to do is pick the right tempo and the right tune. You don't need it, you can do it. Well, Win did it long before I thought of it. And we just enjoyed ourselves and locked that room up, and locked that band up. They were at our feet. That was that night.

We had a date the next afternoon. The next night was an afternoon gig at the other ballroom there. We stayed up all night listening to music and glorying in being together. You know what they got the next afternoon? The bandleader looked at us and said, what happened? Where was the band that knocked us out the night before? We didn't have nothing, we didn't have no enthusiasm, we had no glow, had nothing but tired bodies reporting for duty. And we were a complete flop. We just -- and this was the other side of the coin.
And these are all learning experiences that, if you are going to put music first, then you have to put it first. All along the line, you make it, you're sharp and you make it.
And you don't drag yourself like that. And a good example of that was getting up at 9:00 in the morning, because that's the only time Decca would give us to make a date in 1942.
Oh, that was the first date under your label?
Right.
Yeah,

Right. And I got the date because I had a fan whose father knew Dave Kapp very well. They played cards together, and so he talked to Dave Kapp about getting me a date. And Dave Kapp took my selections, we got a single record that I made for at the time that he was into this kind of thing.

And he took it home with him and played it. And asked his black maid, did that do anything for her, and she says, yeah, that's great. And so I got a date. Otherwise, I wouldn't have got the date. At 9:00 in the morning they gave us a date.

Now, imagine, everybody stayed up, because nobody -- if we worked til 4:00, nobody thought of going home and by the time you go to bed and everything it gets to be 6:00, then you got to get up at 8:00 to get to the studio. So you stayed up. But it was different. Everybody showed up grumpy, growly, but they showed up and they showed up to play. And they played.

Now, although some of us never talked to each other when we left that place, we were spoilsports. And mostly because the engineers, again, like we were talking, set up to suit themselves. They didn't set up to suit us. They muffled the drums and put them over there in the corner, put the piano in another corner, put Murphy -- I think he was playing bass, in another corner, put Eddie somewhere else. We just weren't together like we would be on a job.
Right.
And we thought it was a terrible thing to do. But it turned out that it was one of the best dates we ever made, we ever made at that time.
Did you know Rod Cless?

Yes, Rod Cless on clarinet. And Rod and I -- again, did you know that Rod Cless had been married to Bud Freeman's sister? This I did know, and I think they had a child and they broke up. And, yes, Rod played clarinet with us and he was one of the great clarinet players because, again, the simplicity of his playing.
Yeah. I'd almost forgotten.
He learned to play --
Beautiful player.
He learned to play like Johnny Dodds. People still do not understand, especially a critic who -- I try to use that word kindly, but it's very hard. But they
don't understand. They don't understand the greatness of Johnny Dodds. Because, again, they take him out of context. They listen with deafened ears, they can't listen with ears all the time.
Yeah.

They could hear at the time what was going on. They could hear what he was doing, and hear that no one else was doing it at that time. And that he was playing real New Orleans style clarinet, which -- a clarinet doesn't like Benny Goodman, which -- in part of this number he's playing melody, part he's playing harmony and part he's playing -- the clarinet has a definite third position, just like the -- it's almost like barbershop. There's a melody that's sung out, and there's the bass part and then there's the harmonic part above the melody. And you just stay in a harmonic slot.

And this is what Rod Cless learned so very well, and learned it from Johnny Dodds, although he also admired Jimmy Noone. But he learned it very well. And many people didn't appreciate it, but I did. And you know who was a great fan of his? Bob Seal. And he gave us a date because of Rod Cless. He was a big fan at that time, yeah.
Yeah. It's funny how people have changed and gone on to other things. It's really strange, you know?

They had the truth in their lap, and they said, yeah, that's all right for those times, but we have to go on, we have to progress. The world is in such a state of progress that it's like Stop the world, the cats are killing themselves. Any more progress and we'll be off of this world.
And this is -- I always think the music of the times almost shows the way of the times, the life of the times.
Yeah.

It almost signifies what we're going through. Reflects the times And, of course, I'm getting completely away, but I've always -- for many years I've thought that. But those who don't know are legion. There's just a few that really know. And, of course, the more you know -- it struck me how little they know and how you have to have patience with them, when I went into a shoe store and discovered how little I know about shoes. I said, I don't know a thing about them. I don't know how they're made, I'm not even sure I know my size.

So how can I expect him to know about my thing? And the same with these critics. They are mostly people who like to write for a living, and suddenly they're thrown a job to criticize something they know nothing about. And very few of them will -- if you tell the boss, I know nothing about this, you're out of work. So it's -- let me give you an example.

A mother took her son into a music store for a bass lesson. It happened at noon, and the fellow at the desk hollered out to the back, hey, is there any bass player back there? Who's back there? And the guy answered, just me, I'm a drum teacher. Well, come on out here, you can give this guy a lesson. And he went out there and he gave him a lesson.

one of these places that went door to door, you rent the instrument and get so many lessons, then you can buy the instrument. At a big music store, I was complaining that I didn't have enough drum students. So the guy who was running the program said, well, you play vibes, why don't you teach accordion? I said, I don't play accordion. He says, you just stay a lesson ahead. I said, I can't do that. I can't do something like that.

Yeah. And the funniest experience was much later on, doing electric concert things in high schools. In Wisconsin, I did 88 one winter, in 1964. And I'm at one school and the principal after the concert was talking to me, I think he kind of liked my concert, he's getting kind of intimate, telling stories.

He says, I've got to tell you a story that happened here. He says, we have a teacher that teaches clarinet. And every lesson is, like, two dollars. And he does it in his room there, after school. And this one day he got a call from a hospital, his wife was in the hospital. And he had to rush
out. So he left a note on the music stand. Take the next page and leave your two dollars.
So -- but, anyway, very few people -- the first critic I met was Helen Oakley. She came to the Subway. Just Basie was playing there.
World's longest bar.

World's longest bar. And she came in there and that's the first time I'd heard that there was people who were not musicians that were listening to us. I never thought anybody listened to musicians but other musicians. I suddenly discovered there were a few people here and there.
Well, when did people start coming to hear the music? When did the music become public? We talked earlier about the bands being sort of functional, what went on --
I didn't see it until I got to New York, in '38. I saw it in the Hickory House.
But not in Chicago.
No. Buddy Rich on drums and Joe Marsala at the band, and that's where I saw it.
Yeah. Well, what happened between '31 and '38 in Chicago?
You tried to live those years without eating. That was when the accordion came into being. That was when you went up to see an agent and you said, I got a

little band, and the guys says, what else do you do? Do you wear funny hats? Do you have a dance routine? Do you go around the tables? Do you have some songs? What else do you do? And it had become not enough that you had a band to play music. You had to do something else.
Be in show business.
Show business. And it became a -- that came with the accordion. The accordion came in and the accordion was an instrument that you could go from table to table and play. And play music.
Is there an accordion on one side of that record?
I think there may be on that thing. I think the piano player that day, or somebody sold him on the idea of using it.
I thought you were on the date, too.
No, no.
You weren't on the date with him.
The only date I made with him was the So, little by little, the music was going out the window. Just all sorts of explanations. Radio was coming in.
And the Depression came, too.
And the Depression. And with radio, big bands sound good on radio, little bands don't sound so

good. So they stopped. The big band with the (inaudible). And so we were slowly -- and Louis Armstrong wasn't -- tried doing it by himself and he has having a hard time. I think Red Saunders taught us a little about the hard time that he had trying even to put a hall together and rent a hall and do something to keep his way of life.
Work became very scarce.
Yeah. Well, Louis had gone on the road with Zilner Randolph. Well, he had gone to New York.
Come back.
And Zilner Randolph put together a band and they had a tour of the South.

And for us, then, fortunately for the likes of me, as I can play for entertainers again. And if you could play a show, and I was a very good showman, for those days, for the shows in those days, they were all alike. You didn't have Grecian dance. You had the stripper, you had the fan dancer, you had the MC and you had the vocalist, the snake dancer. What is that?
(Inaudible.)

So, really, it wasn't a big deal to play in those shows. Once in a while they had some music. They had a Spanish dance team. You knew you were in for it. Boy, Spanish dancing is the worst. And you knew you were in for it, and then, some of it you knew you were in for it because the
theme was going to do nothing, usually you were going to play twice as fast as they danced. The work was in the music, not on the floor. And you hated it.
The best acts always had to

But you learned that and you went along. And I got so I was very professional doing that. Without being a great reader, because I never had that music in front of me that much. And I was thrown into that thing. The studios weren't in existence at all then.

So I was very much in demand. I could always -- and the Liberty Inn was like a home. I could always go there. And I wasn't into having my own band. So that kept me -- didn't keep me out of work. The minute you started having your own band, you could forget about working steady.
You had guys following you.

Yeah. You're now in another bag and you really can figure you're going to be out of work a lot. But the minute you start working for anyone, there's all sorts of people that want you, and especially if you can do everything that's called on in a club.
So during those years I could find work because I was playing.
Well, there was a lot of -- the jazz guys in Chicago left in the early '30s.
COTTON CONTENT
Right.
Slowly. Some of them left fast and some took longer to leave.
and everybody.
Yeah, they went to New York. But some of us took a little longer. And I wanted to hear more music.
Why did they go to New York? Was that where the --
Condon went first. But one of them went first, and when he got there, waved his hand to those who were behind. Come quick, you're missing out on a fortune. And this kind of thing.

So they -- the next one was -- and I think it may have been that the Chicagoans went at once. I don't know the history of that. But suddenly, I was lonesome. Suddenly, I was alone. I was with the second line, so to speak. The front guys had left. But to me, I hadn't got enough. I was at the ______ every night. It didn't bother me. I was still able to play with Benny Morland, Earl Murphy -- I can't think of his . Wylie who had the -- he had the band at the Liberty. He was a great dancer. He came up with the . And he also played the ______ shows and tent shows and all, so he knew how to play these kootch numbers. He did the same thing on the bass drum that ______ used the
tom-toms for. Yeah, and he really was great, especially for those times. This is a New York guy.

But suddenly I was left with these people. But I always had the Barbeque to go to and hear these -- so the music was out at the South Side and it was available. And I was like a latecomer who had discovered something out there, and I wasn't ready to quit. And although Downbeat at that time was writing about what was happening in New York, I was getting the feeling that the streets were paved with gold, and here I'm struggling, I wasn't ready to leave. I felt like there was more for me to do than just

There was actually a breakup with some chick that caused me to get ready to change the scenery. And then of course, me and my wife says, well, that's it, I've had it with Chicago and that's playing for singers, I don't care for it. And another thing that turned me off was this cheating.
Like you described earlier.

I'd gotten to be the laughingstock in delivery, because I was playing for the sake of playing, and I'd sit down and entertain with my eyes closed. And they were robbing me blind. It got to be a big joke, out in front, about this guy -- I was still making good dough, but I was interested.
The Liberty Inn, if you started playing at 10:00, you went til 1:00. That means you played a dance, the piano
player, who was me, got up and played for two entertainers. And there was never no money then, no tips. It just had to be done. Pulled the piano back, played another dance.
With the band.

With the band, a quartet or trio, and another piano thing. Back again, then a show. And nothing happened like that until 1:00. By 1:00 you started getting the money people in. Now, the piano player in the bar would be through at -- he would come back and play, but if you wanted to finish, then you could make that money, because that's when the tippers came in, after 1:00.
Well, was Liberty Inn a strippers' joint?
The show, yeah. Everything was -- yeah, strippers show. And then you could make the money. But I wasn't interested. So if I did play, I just played for kicks. I was into jazz now.

And so these gals or whoever -- whatever they wanted to give me, they'd give me because it got to be a big joke. And I lost my taste for that. This dishonesty, the whole thing was galling and I just wanted to play and get half knocked out most of the time on whatever I was on, and just play, play for music's sake, music for the sake of music. Make enough money so you could have your food, pay your rent and all that, self-supporting. But nobody was making that kind
of money so you could retire. You're talking pre-Roosevelt so you're not talking Social Security.

Now, one of the funniest things there was Totts , a piano player and a very fine one. Well, at that time, Roosevelt came in with the Blue Eagle thing. Now, that we should not be unfair to labor and all that. And the Liberty Inn was not that organized, anyway. They were very much against it. And one night, Tut got out -- whatever Rosicrucian or Far Eastern kick he was on, and decided to make a speech. And he told the drummer, give me a roll of the drums.

The drummer gave him a roll, and he upped and made this speech. And .. got Johnny McGovern, who was a tough Irish kid. And we're standing there listening to this guy talk, telling the people not to come in and go away, they were unfair and all that. And he's ready to kill this guy. And McGovern says, don't kill him, shake him. I never seen anything like that. He picked Tut up and just shook him, and shook all that nonsense out of him.

Now, previous to that, Tut was on a backward kick. He would walk into the Liberty Inn backwards. He would -- can you imagine walking into a tough place like that, where people are having an eye-opener and all that, back in through the bar, through the door that leads to the back room, back in, hang up your coat, back --
Walk backwards.

Walk back through the bar, behind the bar to the piano. Everything moved backwards. And they tolerated this at the Liberty Inn. They thought it was queer and they looked at him out of one eye, but they tolerated it. It helped the atmosphere, gave it a laugh, something.
Tut's still pretty odd.

But until he made that speech, everything was great. They tolerated him. But with that speech, it's funny how that -- everything turned around and he was walking frontwards and all that, just with Johnny shaking him. I got the story from Earl Wiley. I wasn't there at the time. Tut was working there. But it was that kind of a place, where they let you -- one time, Earl Wiley drank to excess many times. When he drank, he drank to excess. And then he couldn't play, and he knew it.

And then you had to follow him. They loved him there. So that, one of the bosses would send -- or do it themselves, see what Earl would do, because Earl would break down his drums. That's a modern term, tear down his drums. And pawn them so he'd get enough money. And they'd follow him and get the pawn tickets, and redeem them there, and he'd be working -- you know he'd been working . But he'd just get so drunk, that this one night, Dave T ough was visiting. And it was early in the evening. Earl was upstairs drinking and Dave was downstairs.

So they got Dave to sit in. After one set, they went up and got Earl. And they says, Dave is drunker than you are, come on down and finish the evening. But this -- one time I looked down at the bandstand, and we had Paul , we had Martie Marcella, we had this trumpet player from New Orleans that had spent years in Vegas, Louis Prima, and William . Four trumpets at the same time on stage, with Pee Wee used to come in all the time and sit in there.
It was a great place to sit in, it was a great place to drink and play music. They charged us five cents for a shot of gin.

1946 or '45 . We were in high school together in , and we made a pilgrimage to Chicago to McGovern's Liberty Inn. Had the sign along that wall, and I still have the pictures we took of each other in McGovern's Liberty Inn. Reading about it in the

Some of the things I've read that were written about the happenings, they were very strange happenings. McGovern -- the old man was from the old school. He was a big Irish -- slim, pretty slim, a little bit of a paunch but not much. And I imagine at that time he was over 70, but still very spry and active.
And he liked to have women around, so the was always full of women that had nowhere to go in life,

just Waltzing Matilda. So they'd be sitting around and he'd probably make sure they'd get a bunk or get fed, and wait for a live one. A live one would come in and sit down at that bar. That was the end, if he had any money, because the parade would start.

I'd be playing behind the bar and the parade started. First one girl would walk behind the bar, maybe just rub it a little, and he'd pay no attention. Guy's drinking his Irish whiskey. But after about two or three times like that, he looks around and finally he sees something and says, hey, how about giving her a drink? So she's standing there having a drink with him . In no time, he's buying seven drinks and buying me one which is going down the drain. Everybody. He's drinking the best. And the next thing you know --
Everyone else is drinking watered Cokes.

Yeah, but he's drinking the best. And pretty soon he's got -- but they got the upstairs. So somebody leads him upstairs and he gets them a bed to sleep on and all that. The chances are that when he wakes up the next day, he's got carfare or something. I don't say they reached in his pockets, although they might have.
But the point is that he might have got them to spend all that he had. How long can you last buying nine, ten drinks
a round? And they get very thirsty, drinking that colored water. My gosh, that was good, let's have another.
Yeah.

And he was drinking real whisky. So it was a colorful place of its time. Another thing about McGovern's, they didn't mind having a fight there at all. That was a nice activity, to break up the monotony, you know? And even if it cleared the house, it was fun, fun and games. Let's somebody come and start something, wow, they were all over the bar. And the nearest thing I saw to that was the Brass Rail in 1957.

I've seen the owner clear the place of business, and start after some college kids, four college football players, thought they could tear the joint up. Went in the bathroom and took the towels and everything. And the boss got after them, one blow led to another, the bartender is over there with the little thing that he hits them over the head to get their attention. And out in the street they're fighting and everybody has cleared the place and no one is thinking about the business that they're losing and all that. They're all so involved in the fight, see.
It's like something I've never seen. Looks like the olden days. Very few places would do that. Too many bosses are aware of registers ringing.
Take them out quietly.

HEMLOCK
MR. HODES: Get them out quietly. And then in the
old days, of course, --
MR. DEMICHAEL: Well, Chicago was a rough-and-tumble
town.
MR. HODES: But I've seen them give mickeys. I've
seen a policeman get a mickey, and take his two guns out or
one gun -- I think it was one gun -- and just lay it on the
bar. He knew he'd had it. He was just -- what is the word,
obstreperous? He was a pain in the rear end. And they didn't
know how else to handle him because he was a policeman. So
they gave him a drink.
And then you know what they did for humor's sake?
They packed the toilets. They saw that the people were waiting

Yes, Rod Kessel on clarinet. And Rod and I -- again, did you know that Rod K... had been married to Bud Freeman's sister? This I did know, and I think they had a child and they broke up. And, yes, Rod played clarinet with us and he was one of the great clarinet players because, again, the simplicity of his playing.
Yeah. And almost forgotten now.
He learned to play --
Beautiful player.
He learned to play like Johnny Dodds. People still do not understand, especially a critic who -- I try to use that word kindly, but it's very hard. But they
don't understand. They don't understand the greatness of Johnny Dodds. Because, again, they take him out of context. They listen with different ears, they can't listen with ears of that time.
Yeah.

They could hear at the time what was going on. They could hear what he was doing, and hear that no one else was doing it at that time. And that he was playing real New Orleans style clarinet, which -- a clarinet doesn't play like Benny Goodman, which -- in part of this number he's playing melody, part he's playing harmony and part he's playing -- the clarinet has a definite third position, just like the -- it's almost like barbershop. There's a melody that's sung out, and there's the bass part and then there's the harmonic part above the melody. And you just stay in a harmonic slot.

And this is what Rod Cless learned so very well, and learned it from Johnny Dodds, although he also admired Jimmy Noone. But he learned it very well. And many people didn't appreciate it, but I did. And you know who was a great fan of his? Bob Thiele And he gave us a date because of Rod Cless. He was a big fan at that time, yeah.
With a trio, wasn't it? (With [Jimmy] Butts on bass?)
Yeah. It's funny how people have changed and gone on to other things. It's really strange, you know?

They had the truth in their lap, and they said, yeah, that's all right for those times, but we have to go on, we have to progress. The world is in such a state of progress that it's like Wngy Manone Sad Stop the world, the cats are killing themselves. Any more progress and we'll be off of this world.
And this is -- I always think the music of the times almost shows the way of the times, the life of the times.
Yeah.

It almost signifies what we're going through. Reflects the times. almost . And, of course, I'm getting completely away, but I've always -- for many years I've thought that. But those who don't know are legion. There's just a few that really know. And, of course, the more you know -- it struck me how little they know and how you have to have patience with them, when I went into a shoe store and discovered how little I know about shoes. I said, I don't know a thing about them. I don't know how they're made, I'm not even sure I know my size.

So how can I expect him to know about my thing? And the same with these critics. They are mostly people who like to write for a living, and suddenly they're thrown a job to criticize something they know nothing about. And very few of them will -- if you tell the boss, I know nothing about this, you're out of work. So it's -- let me give you an example.

A mother took her son into a music store for a bass lesson. It happened at noon, and the fellow at the desk hollered out to the back, hey, is there any bass player back there? Who's back there? And the guy answered, just me, I'm a drum teacher. Well, come on out here, you can give this guy a lesson. And he went out there and he gave him a lesson.
Yeah that happened to me, when I didn't have enough drum students. And I was complaining -- you get me more drum students -- this was in Louisville

one of these places that went door to door, you rent the instrument and get so many lessons, then you can buy the instrument. At a big music store, I was complaining that I didn't have enough drum students. So the guy who was running the program said, well, you play vibes, why don't you teach accordion? I said, I don't play accordion. He says, you just stay a lesson ahead. I said, I can't do that. I can't do something like that.

Yeah. And the funniest experience was much later on, doing electric concert things in high schools. In Wisconsin, I did 88 one winter, in 1964. And I'm at one school and the principal after the concert was talking to me, I think he kind of liked my concert, he's getting kind of intimate, telling stories.

He says, I've got to tell you a story that happened here. He says, we have a teacher that teaches clarinet. And every lesson is, like, two dollars. And he does it in his room there, after school. And this one day he got a call from a hospital, his wife was in the hospital. And he had to rush
out. So he left a note on the music stand. Take the next page and leave your two dollars.
So -- but, anyway, very few people -- the first critic I met was Helen Oakley. She came to the Subway. Jess Stacy was playing there.
World's longest bar.

World's longest bar. And she came in there and that's the first time I'd heard that there was people who were not musicians that were listening to us. I never thought anybody listened to musicians but other musicians. I suddenly discovered there were a few people here and there.
Well, when did people start coming to hear the music? When did the music become public? We talked earlier about the bands being sort of functional, what went on --
I didn't see it until I got to New York, in '38. I saw it in the Hickory House.
But not in Chicago.
No. Buddy Rich on drums and Joe Marsala at the band, and that's where I saw it.
Yeah. Well, what happened between '31 and '38 in Chicago?
You tried to live those years without eating. That was when the accordion came into being. That was when you went up to see an agent and you said, I got a

little band, and the guy says, what else do you do? Do you wear funny hats? Do you have a dance routine? Do you go around the tables? Do you have some songs? What else do you do? And it had become not enough that you had a band to play music. You had to do something else.
Be in show business.
Show business. And it became a -- that came with the accordion. The accordion came in and the accordion was an instrument that you could go from table to table and play. And play music.
Is there an accordion on one side of that Wingy Manone record?
I think there may be on that 'My Cellar' thing. I think he have found might not the piano player that day, or somebody sold him on the idea of using it.
I thought you were on the date, too.
No, no.
You weren't on the date with him.
The only date I made with him was the Vocation --. So, little by little, the music was going out the window. Just all sorts of explanations. Radio was coming in.
And the Depression came, too.
And the Depression. And with radio, big bands sound good on radio, little bands don't sound so

good. So they stopped. The big band with the fullness of it. And so we were slowly -- and Louis Armstrong wasn't -- tried doing it by himself and he has having a hard time. I think Red Saunders taught us a little about the hard time that he had trying even to put a hall together and rent a hall and do something to keep his way of life.
Work became very scarce.
Yeah. Well, Louis had gone on the road with Zilner Randolph. Well, he had gone to New York.
Come back.
And Zilner Randolph put together a band and they had a tour of the South.

And for us, then, fortunately for the likes of me, as I can play for entertainers again. And if you could play a show, and I was a very good showman, for those days, for the shows in those days, they were all alike. You didn't have Grecian dance. You had the stripper, you had the fan dancer, you had the MC and you had the vocalist, the snake dancer. What is that?
I went through the same thing in Louisville.

So, really, it wasn't a big deal to play in those shows. Once in a while they had some music. They had a Spanish dance team. You knew you were in for it. Boy, Demichael; to read. -Black. Hodes; Spanish dancing is the worst. And you knew you were in for it, and then, some of it you knew you were in for it because the
theme was going to do nothing, usually you were going to play twice as fast as they danced. The work was in the music, not on the floor. And you hated it.
The best acts always had the easiest instruments.

But you learned that and you went along. And I got so I was very professional doing that. Without being a great reader, because I never had that music in front of me that much. And I was thrown into that thing. The studios weren't in existence at all then.

So I was very much in demand. I could always -- and the Liberty Inn was like a home. I could always go there. And I wasn't into having my own band. So that kept me -- didn't keep me out of work. The minute you started having your own band, you could forget about working steady.
You had guys following you.

Yeah. You're now in another bag and you really can figure you're going to be out of work a lot. But the minute you start working for anyone, there's all sorts of people that want you, and especially if you can do everything that's called on in a club.
So during those years I could find work because I was playing.
Well, there was a lot of -- the jazz guys in Chicago left in the early '30s.
Right.
Bud, the McPartands -- I guess just Jimmy left -- Bix.
Slowly. Some of them left fast and some took longer to leave.
Krupa and Condon and everybody.
Yeah, they went to New York. But some of us took a little longer. And I wanted to hear more music.
Why did they go to New York? Was that where the -- (recording interruption)
Condon went first. But one of them went first, and when he got there, waved his hand to those who were behind. Come quick, you're missing out on a fortune. And this kind of thing.

So they -- the next one was -- and I think it may have been that the Chicagoans went at once. I don't know the history of that. But suddenly, I was lonesome. Suddenly, I was alone. I was with the second line, so to speak. The front guys had left. But to me, I hadn't got enough. I was at the Barbecue every night. It didn't bother me. I was still able to play with Denny Morland, Earl Murphy -- I can't number. I wrote him up in the Jazz Record, think of his Drummer Earl Wylie who had the -- he had the band at the Liberty. He was a great dancer. He came up with the riverboats. And he also played the Stock shows and tent shows and all, so he knew how to play these kootch numbers. He did the same thing on the bass drum that they used the
tom-toms for. Yeah, and he really was great, especially for those times. This is a New York guy.

But suddenly I was left with these people. But I always had the Barbeque to go to and hear these -- so the music was out at the South Side and it was available. And I was like a latecomer who had discovered something out there, and I wasn't ready to quit. And although DownBeat at that time was writing about what was happening in New York, I was getting the feeling that the streets were paved with gold, and here I'm struggling, I wasn't ready to leave. I felt like there was more for me to do than just whatever it was.

There was actually a breakup with some chick that caused me to get ready to change the scenery. And then of course, me and my wife says, well, that's it, I've had it with Chicago and that's playing for singers, I don't care for it. And another thing that turned me off was this cheating.
Like you described earlier.

I'd gotten to be the laughingstock in delivery, because I was playing for the sake of playing, and I'd sit down and entertain with my eyes closed. And they were robbing me blind. It got to be a big joke, out in front, about this guy -- I was still making good dough, but I wasn't interested.
The Liberty Inn, if you started playing at 10:00, you went til 1:00. That means you played a dance, the piano
player, who was me, got up and played for two entertainers. And there was never no money then, no tips. It just had to be done. Then you pulled the piano back, played another dance.
With the band.

With the band, a quartet or trio, and another piano thing. Back again, then a show. And nothing happened like that until 1:00. By 1:00 you started getting the money people in. Now, the piano player in the bar would be through at -- he would come back and play, but if you wanted to finish, then you could make that money, because that's when the tippers came in, after 1:00.
Well, was Liberty Inn a strippers' joint?
The show, yeah. Everything was -- yeah, strippers show. And then you could make the money. But I wasn't interested. So if I did play, I just played for kicks. I was into jazz now.

And so these gals or whoever -- whatever they wanted to give me, they'd give me because it got to be a big joke. And I lost my taste for that. This dishonesty, the whole thing was galling and I just wanted to play and get half knocked out most of the time on whatever I was on, and just play, play for music's sake, music for the sake of music. Make enough money so you could have your food, pay your rent and all that, self-supporting. But nobody was making that kind
of money so you could retire. You're talking pre-Roosevelt so you're not talking Social Security.

Now, one of the funniest things there was Totts Scott, a piano player and a very fine one. Well, at that time, Roosevelt came in with the Blue Eagle thing. Now, that we should not be unfair to labor and all that. And the Liberty Inn was not that organized, anyway. They were very much against it. And one night, Tut got out -- whatever Rosicrucian or Far Eastern kick he was on, and decided to make a speech. And he told the drummer, give me a roll of the drums.

The drummer gave him a roll, and he upped and made this speech. And one of the help got Johnny McGovern, who was a tough Irish kid. And we're standing there listening to this guy talk, telling the people not to come in and go away, they were unfair and all that. And he's ready to kill this guy. And McGovern says, don't kill him, shake him. I never seen anything like that. He picked Tut up and just shook him, and shook all that nonsense out of him.

Now, previous to that, Tut was on a backward kick. He would walk into the Liberty Inn backwards. He would -- can you imagine walking into a tough place like that, where people are having an eye-opener and all that, back in through the bar, through the door that leads to the back room, back in, hang up your coat, back --
Walk backwards.

Walk back through the bar, behind the bar to the piano. Everything moved backwards. And they tolerated this at the Liberty Inn. They thought it was queer and they looked at him out of one eye, but they tolerated it. It helped the atmosphere, gave it a laugh, something.
Tut's still pretty odd.

But until he made that speech, everything was great. They tolerated him. But with that speech, it's funny how that -- everything turned around and he was walking frontwards and all that, just with Johnny shaking him. I got the story from Earl Wiley. I wasn't there at the time. Tut was working there. But it was that kind of a place, where they let you -- one time, Earl Wiley drank to excess many times. When he drank, he drank to excess. And then he couldn't play, and he knew it.

And then you had to follow him. They loved him there. So that, one of the bosses would send -- or do it themselves, see what Earl would do, because Earl would break down his drums. That's a modern term, tear down his drums. And pawn them so he'd get enough money. And they'd follow him and get the pawn tickets, and redeem them later, and he'd be working -- you know he'd been working out from behind. But he'd just get so drunk, that this one night, Dave Tough was visiting. And it was early in the evening. Earl was upstairs drinking and Dave was downstairs.

So they got Dave to sit in. After one set, they went up and got Earl. And they says, 'Your self' is drunker than you are, come on down and finish the evening. But this -- one time I looked down at the bandstand, and we had Paul Mares, we had Martie Marcella, we had this trumpet player from New Orleans that had spent years in Vegas, Louis Prima, and Wingy Manone. Four trumpets at the same time on stage, with Wettling. Pee Wee used to come in all the time and sit in there.
It was a great place to sit in, it was a great place to drink and play music. They charged us five cents for a shot of gin.

1946 or '45. Gilbert Erskine's Friend of. We were in high school together in Louisville, and we made a pilgrimage to Chicago to McGovern's Liberty Inn. Had the sign along that wall, and I still have the pictures we took of each other by McGovern's Liberty Inn. Reading about it in the Jazz Record.

Some of the things I've read that were written about the happenings, they were very strange happenings. McGovern -- the old man was from the old school. He was a big Irish -- slim, pretty slim, a little bit of a paunch but not much. And I imagine at that time he was over 70, but still very spry and active.
And he liked to have women around, so the (Unintelligible) was always full of women that had nowhere to go in life,

just Waltzing Matilda. So they'd be sitting around and he'd probably make sure they'd get a bunk or get fed, and wait for a live one. A live one would come in and sit down at that bar. That was the end, if he had any money, because the parade would start.

I'd be playing behind the bar and the parade started. First one girl would walk behind the bar, maybe just rub it a little, and he'd pay no attention. Guy's drinking his Irish whiskey. But after about two or three times like that, he looks around and finally he sees something and says, hey, how about giving her a drink? So she's standing there having a drink with him —hey man, how about my friend? In no time, he's buying seven drinks and buying me one which is going down the drain. Everybody. He's drinking the best. And the next thing you know --
Everyone else is drinking watered Cokes.

Yeah, but he's drinking the best. And pretty soon he's got -- but they got the upstairs. So somebody leads him upstairs and he gets them a bed to sleep on and all that. The chances are that when he wakes up the next day, he's got carfare or something. I don't say they reached in his pockets, although they might have.
But the point is that he might have got them to spend all that he had. How long can you last buying nine, ten drinks
a round? And they get very thirsty, drinking that colored water. My gosh, that was good, let's have another.
Yeah.

And he was drinking real whisky. So it was a colorful place of its time. Another thing about McGovern's, they didn't mind having a fight there at all. That was a nice activity, to break up the monotony, you know? And even if it cleared the house, it was fun, fun and games. Let somebody come and start something, wow, they were all over the bar. And the nearest thing I saw to that was the Brass Rail in 1957.

I've seen the owner clear the place of business, and start after some college kids, four college football players, thought they could tear the joint up. I went in the bathroom in the toilet, and took the towels and everything and threw 'em. And the boss got after them, one blow led to another, the bartender is over there with the little thing that he hits them over the head to get their attention. And out in the street they're fighting and everybody has cleared the place and no one is thinking about the business that they're losing and all that. They're all so involved in the fight, see.
It's like something I've never seen. Looks like the olden days. Very few places would do that. Too many bosses are aware of registers ringing.
Take them out quietly.
Get them out quietly. And then in the old days, of course, --
Well, Chicago was a rough-and-tumble town.

But I've seen them give mickeys. I've seen a policeman get a mickey, and take his two guns out or one gun -- I think it was one gun -- and just lay it on the bar. He knew he'd had it. He was just -- what is the word, obstreperous? He was a pain in the rear end. And they didn't know how else to handle him because he was a policeman. So they gave him a drink.

And then you know what they did for humor's sake? They packed the toilets. They saw that the people were waiting in line to get in the toilets, where they were full. And the cop had to go out in the alley, didn't know which way to go, whether to heave or to shit, as the word is. And they were standing on the laughing at him and there was nothing he could do. Because he knew he'd gotten it.
He might could do something the next day, but he couldn't do nothing then, he just handed over his gun.
Well, then, you spent most of your time working at the Liberty Inn.
Liberty Inn or places like that. I can't name them all.
What decided you to go to New York,
the breakup or --

Well, actually, I'd read so much about New York by this time. And all the players that were making it there, and that the streets were paved with gold. And I couldn't believe it. These guys were down here doing nothing, and I was getting lonesome. Accordionists were taking all the jobs and I wasn't eating too good. It was getting so I'd put a band together just to rehearse.

We'd go into a bar and there'd be a piano there and we asked the band if we could play. Said, go ahead. And we'd play and buy our own drinks, til we got tired of playing. People would look at us like we're nuts. But we had to have a place to play, and we'd go there. And enough of these scenes, and you get tired, man. You're not --
Ain't happening.

It's not happening. Chicago became a ghost town. There was no jazz anymore. So eventually it came to my mind it was time to pack up and go. But it just happened that at that time I met my wife. It just worked out perfect. We decided to make a honeymoon out of it. Rather, I decided.
41 years ago. You celebrated your anniversary yesterday.
Right. Pack all your things -- can you imagine, a little Ford, two-door Ford, two dogs, all your

personal belongings, hers and yours, all in the inside of that car, and you drive to New York. As that prizefighter, Bill Canady, said, Herbs, you get to New York, you got a place to stay. You belong in New York. Herbs, -- that's what they used to -- New Orleans guys. Didn't say Pops all the time, just say Herbs. I don't know why. It's just the same as "pass the post." I never knew what that meant. That means you go around the counter, somebody's got a fist in your mouth.
They had their own language. So I believed him. And he was right. I went to New York and got an apartment, a basement apartment, and he gave us a home for three months so I could get started.
That's like a watershed, the Chicago period, and then when you went to New York.
Yeah, complete break with the town, break with --
A new life, you were married.

And I was working at the Liberty Inn when I told them I was leaving. And one of the McGoverns, a woman, she says, I don't believe this. You got a steady job here, you're making $35 a week, you're going off in the unknown, how can you do this? And she couldn't understand that.
And the thing was appalling on me, there's no life there anymore, it was just a job. I will always remember, there was a clarinet player at that time I was working

for at the Liberty Inn who was Johnny Lane. He's still playing that kind of. And Johnny would sit there, a nice little potbelly around, Italian but he changed it, just like Frankie Lane from Italiano to Lane. And he's standing there playing the clarinet and here comes this stripper. And he's playing her music.

And at the end of the act she takes her bow. And the fans go out and the rear end sticks back. And here's. Johnny with his clarinet almost in her rear end, his eyes pop out and the show was watching Johnny pop his eyes out seeing that big rear end. It's like a drummer once said to me, working at this place, I'm getting so tired of seeing naked women, I appreciate seeing a naked man.
Must feel like a doctor.
They all pass in review in front of you, it's the untouchables.
I played strippers for two years, seven nights a week. And I feel like a doctor. Nothing.
And begin the whole business -- started getting to you where you're not -- nothing is happening, really. All the guys are in New York, making it.
Nothing was happening much musically, either.
And so I said, okay, I'm going to go. And I quit. And packed the car up and made the trip.
(Recording interruption)
We'll start right there.

Well, if you can imagine the -- a couple, just married, two dogs and the Ford full of all our possessions, our few records, just packed, you could barely see out of it. And we're in New York, and there we are. We're in this big town and we find our way way up North there, the Washington-something, where Bill Kennedy was living. And he's over there with open arms, come on in, a basement apartment, very little privacy, especially for a newly married couple. It's very embarrassing. Because she'd already gotten pregnant. So she couldn't wait to get out and get our own place. Within three months, she did.

But the next day I am on the subway, I'm taught how to go there, and I'm down on Elm, which is a main stem at night. No; I went to the union first and deposited my card, and they told me the whereabouts, what to do. Now, you can't do this and you can't do that and you can't do this. By the time they got through telling me all the can'ts, you feel like leaving town. Because --
You can't work out of town.

No, you can't work one night on a steady gig, at that time. They wouldn't get you do that, either. Plus, I found out later on that most of the leaders were instructed not to encourage out of town men by giving them work. Their whole idea --
So you didn't have anything pending or anything.

Nothing. I was in bad shape. We just had to scrape. So I went down and put my card in, but I knew Joe Marsala, I called him up. He says, come on down. So I went down to see what the street was. And this was my first shot.
52nd Street?
52nd Street. He was working there with -- and he had Buddy Rich on drums. I don't remember the other people. Oh, and we had Marty Marsala on trumpet.
You had Adelle --

Yes, and we had Adelle playing the harp. And people were paying to come and to listen. Now, you can imagine the shock that is to a musician who's always played on a stage for a stripper or an M.C. or a snake dancer, or some sort of act, which the band was to be heard but not seen, essentially.

And here, the whole thing is visual. You're up there being looked at and listened to. And no one's dancing. I just couldn't believe this was happening. And immediately, Joe says, come to work for me. And I said, but the union system -- I don't know if he used those words, 'fringe the union', but words to that effect. Come on, anyway.
Well, who was I to say no? I mean, -- and I sat
in and got my first writeup in DownBeat. A new pianist that hit New York and set the Hickory House on its rear end. He's got to take the town apart, he's that great. One of those things.
Who was playing piano there?
That I don't remember, either.
Joe Bushkin was around.

No, he hadn't arrived yet, he hadn't come in. I was -- and Joe hadn't come on the scene yet. Bushkin hadn't arrived. So the next night, I did bring the tuxedo with me, because in Chicago at that time there were so many jobs that called for a tuxedo and you had to own one. The revolution didn't come til later.
It's not complete yet.

As you say, it's not complete yet. So I had my tux, and just -- wouldn't you know it, just as I'm ready to leave Bill's house, here comes the delegation from the union. Knocks on the door. Oh, are you Art Hodes? Yeah, yeah. Well, glad to have you in New York. You're dressed up, where are you going? I says, I've been invited to a wedding. What would you say? I ducked him.
I got on that train, that suburb, whatever it was, and I got to -- but by the time I got to the Hickory House, I was a basket case.
Because of the union?

Because of the union. I could feel its presence on my back. And I could see myself being -- if they catch you doing that, you immediately have your card lifted, and you cannot come back to that town for one year. You can't put your card in again.
How long had you been there?

I'd been there just a matter of days. I couldn't see losing that. And within days, I'd gotten an offer from -- the word had gotten around that I'd sat in, and that I was good. Bunny Berigan gave me an offer to join him, but he was leaving town, and I didn't want to leave town and lose --
You had to stay in town in order --
To get my union card. I wanted that New York union card, so I could work in the union. That's why I came. I didn't come to join a band and leave, even though it was tempting to be with Bunny Berigan.

So here I am, out of work. I'm too nervous to keep that job. I played that night, but I played with my head turned, watching the window and all that. It just wasn't worth it. And so I thanked Joe for the chance, and he told me to keep coming in. And it was there that Frankie Laine was singing. He was down on his ass, so to speak, and Joe was just kind enough to hand him a chance for, like, say, five dollars.
He was from Chicago too.

He was from Cleveland. But he'd been -- I didn't think he needed Frankie Laine at all. But Joe was that kind of kind person. He just -- he needs the air time, give him a break. And so he let him sing. And that's where we met. I'd come in there a couple of times, and he'd sing and I'd play. We were both out or work, so he thought it was -- I might be getting a little ahead, but I'd like to get this part, because he thought it would be a good idea that two can do better what one can't seem to do. Let's join forces.

So we became a team called Laine and Hodes, which always irritated me at that time because I thought it should be Hodes and Laine. In fact, when we got the team up to the point where we'd make $50 a week apiece, it became too much for us.
When and where was this?

This was in New York between the years of 1938 and about '40. And we did work. We took jobs in Passaic, New Jersey, and we took a five dollar apiece job to sing for one night or something. We did anything to work. And we did find some work, because Frankie was the kind of guy that would charm the office girl. And he'd say to me, don't you go up there, let me go up there, I'll charm her. And he'd get to see the manager or the booking office man. And so that's what he would do and turn it on, and -- but he was always good to me. The only bone of contention was that. I like the way

he sang. I wasn't ecstatic about it but I liked the way he sang, because he swung. He could swing. And at that time, it's not the Frankie Laine you hear now, he didn't have arrangements or any thing. Everything was off the cuff. Sing two choruses and the piano would take one, and sing another one.
And you hadn't known him in Chicago.

Never met him before. So here we were in New York, struggling with these kind of jobs. I did know a trumpet player by the name of Dick Donahue in Chicago. We had worked at Harry's New York Bar in Chicago, for Floyd Town and His Men About Town. That was another band in Chicago that gave us work.

And Donahue was the kind of trumpet player that, if you needed a first trumpet player, he was the man to get. He could do just about anything he wanted to do. And on top of that he could write. So I would make the arrangements for the band, especially the blues types, and he would just pass out all the parts. He knew how to write. At that time, I didn't.

So Donahue -- three months after we got there, about three months, we got an apartment, but no money. And then pretty soon a baby was on the way. Pretty soon the baby was born. I like the way my wife always relates it. If you can imagine, she says, going into the butcher shop on Christmas to get three pork chops for our Christmas dinner, and then after the man weighed them out, telling them to take one back.
I don't have the money to pay for it. So she says, you could -- so she took off and went back to Chicago with the baby, and left me with Donahue.

So Donahue was a great cook. And by that time, we knew quite a few Chicago musicians and they would all find us, because Donahue would go out and get a -- first he would get a 25 cent bottle of wine, and then he'd get ten cents worth of cloves and ten cents worth of this and that, and a little meat, and he'd make some sort of stew. And as he was making the stew, he would turn the spoon around, add a little wine, taste it, take a drink of wine, add a little wine, taste it. And this went on, and that stew was just out of this world, and that was the only meal we had all day. And we shared it with musicians.

But these were the days. I also discovered a place called Jimmy Ross' Tavern. And Jimmy Ross had gone through -- up in Notre Dame. But what do you do after you graduate from Notre Dame? You open up a tavern. And you got your own tavern. And he had a beatup upright piano down in the basement and he'd let me come in there and play. And I tried to attract a lot of other people to come down there and jam, but Wingy came down and took one look at the place, turned up his nose and never came back again, because that was no place. Nobody would see him there.
But the people that liked to play for kicks and
enjoyed it would come down. George Zack, for example, people like that. Some black players, too. I can't remember all their names.
Where was this?

Jimmy Ross' Tavern was on 6th Avenue, and I think either 51st or 50th. But it was right there, not too far from everything, all the happenings. But the people who did find us was the aficionados that were hovering around the jazz movement. There was a great jazz movement in New York at that time. Kids from Columbia University -- Gene Williams, Ralph Gleason, George Avakian was around, I can name so many more that don't come to mind right now. But the whole movement was happening right then. They discovered jazz. Milt Gabler was putting out records, the Commodores, Steve Smith was putting them out for HRS Rag, and although you couldn't buy the records on the counter, they were always pulled out from behind the counter to those knowing few. And there was a movement there, an excitement. And I became part of it.

There was a magazine called Jazz Information, and I was enthralled with this, that there was people that were so crazy about this music. Because that never happened in Chicago. The only -- you see, the blacks had their people to play for, but the whites didn't have it. The white audience was the Wayne King audience, what we have now, the Lawrence Welk audience, is what we had then, in the Wayne King audience.

If you played jazz, you were persona non grata. And if you played your music at night on that Victrola, you better turn it down real soft, and even use a pin for a needle, because if it got too loud, the neighbors would call the law, that noise, they couldn't stand that noise.

Well, this for a lad coming to New York and seeing this was too much. I just fell right into the scene. I was like made for it. And so I became involved. But meanwhile, the business of making a living. The business of finding a job on Staten Island, playing for the madam. She was really a washed-up broad with much years and much mileage, and people just came to laugh about it.
Would she sing?

But she got out on the floor and did some little song and danced around as if she was 30 instead of twice that age, and hair was unruffled. People came in and it was a joke. But I found myself there, working as part of a trio. But enough money to bring something back. I also found a job called Shibe's, and this because of the statute of limitations I can talk about, too.

That job, after -- (recording interrupted) a place called Shive's, in part of the Village, probably the lower part of the Village, going on toward Chinatown. I got this job through Dick Donahue. Dick Donahue, the trumpet player, knew the drummer, and the drummer -- I think the drummer was Joe

Grasso who later did some things with us. I'm not sure, but I think so. But in any case, the drummer had an uncle who was a union delegate. So he had some clout. And he told us not to worry about nothing, we were safe.

But the pay was a big, fat $18 for six nights, three dollars a night, which made it because we had nothing. And between Dick and I we had six dollars. And wine at 25 cents a bottle, you could see we could get by and not be too --. Well, about the fourth day, I came to work and I noticed they were picketing the place. My union was picketing the place. I says, oh, I can't, this is too much, and I need the money. What are they doing? So when the picket separated and went in opposite directions, I put my -- at that time I did wear a hat, I pulled my hat down over my head and my collar up, and I ran in.

And the band, the trio was there, and they told me not to worry again. Everybody tells me not to worry. But so that night -- it was just a question of running between the pickets. But either the next night or the night after, it didn't really matter, because the boss had let the whole band go. I came to work, I looked up and I said to the boss, where's the band? He says, there is no band. I says, what happened? He says, well, I had to let them go. It's just you today.
So I'm sitting up there, playing the piano, and a

party of about -- I'm guessing, it might have been a dozen people or 18 people, either six couples of whatever, nine couples, came in. And they sat and sat and sat, and finally I'm still part of the business, I went up to the bar and says, where's the waiter, and he says, you're the waiter.

Well, that was a fast engagement for me, as a waiter, although it didn't last either as a pianist. I went up and got the orders. And, of course, I'd never been a waiter, so I got all their drinks all right, but when I came back, it was -- man, I didn't know what drink went to anybody, and the cat said to me, real kindly, he says, why don't you just put the tray down with the drinks, we'll figure it out, you go up there and play the piano. That was it.

But that job didn't last long. I'd say we stayed there maybe two weeks or so. But we really -- this was the scuffling in New York, to try to get your union card together, so that you could stay there six months and get that card. And so this possibly happened in the first three months or the last three months, where I really had to scuffle and do whatever had to be done to make it go.

Now, whether that law was right or wrong, I don't know, that they put up that high tariff. And it's not only in New York. I have a great admiration for the Local in New York. They're a very -- they see way out, they don't just see the view close up to the eye. Chicago, when I got back to

Chicago, they told me at the union, now, you've been to New York and we don't do things like New York or Los Angeles. So before you do anything, you come up here and ask. And the attitude in New York was, go ahead and do it. And if it's not right, we'll either catch you or we'll tell you. But they didn't say, don't do it.

And so I was at one place six months before the delegation came up and said to me, we know you're there, we've been knowing you're there. You haven't come up and told us, but we know you're there. We figured to give you a chance to get this thing started. And that was Pee Wee (and Art's) Back Room. Gave us six months.
Pee Wee and Art's --
Back Room. Pee Wee Russell and I started a club called Pee Wee and Art's Back Room. We're both on our bottoms, no money, walking the streets.
When was this?

This was 1949. It was the Riviera Lounge. Kitty corner from Nick's. And Pee Wee said to me as we -- we didn't have money to walk from 5and Street to the Village -- to drive. The fare was five cents, something like that. So we couldn't spare it.
This was 1949?
1949. So we walked. It might have been ten cents. But it was very minimal. And we walked there.

And on the way, Pee Wee says, I know a man. I says, let's stop in, so we stopped in to see him. And he had a bar, it was the Back Room. And there was nothing happening in the Back Room. So Pee Wee says, how about letting us have the Back Room? And the boss says, fine, it's yours, go ahead and do whatever you want with it.

So he put up a sign above his awning, Pee Wee and Art's Back Room. And within the end of the week, he gave us $30 a week apiece. Meanwhile, we were hiring a bass player, Herb Ward, at $75 a week. So we'd have a trio. At least, two would play and then Pee Wee would come in and so forth. So anyway, we lasted over a year, and then that whole year we booked Jack Teagarden with his band and Louis Armstrong was having his teeth taken out or fixed and the band was laid off. Jack did a week, did eight days there. And that was a real --
MR. DEMICHAEL: I never knew , never read anything about it.

MR. HODES: Almost immediately we got Chippy Hill to come and sing. And then we got Willie Lion Smith. So we had Willie Lion Smith playing opposite me. As Barney Bigard says when he came in there, I like to come in there and see you two guys bumping heads. I never thought I was doing any bumping of heads, because I was in awe of Willie. And I sat there and listened to him play, and every key in the piano he could start a tune.

And there was a trumpet player would come in, an Italian fellow, that we called Face, because of his face, the look on his face, the -- whatever God gave him as a face, it was something different. But Face wanted to play trombone. And Willie was most kind. Willie could only So pretty soon Willie would start changing keys, and Face couldn't make that.

But otherwise, Willie would say, okay, boy, go out and get me some cigars, and give him some money and get rid of him. But Willie was an education, just listening to them play, he was a real tremendous stride pianist that knew so many tunes, he was a composer, too, and I didn't think I was bumping any heads with this one. And Pee Wee and I played together and then I played with the bass player, opposite Willie.
Now, we lasted there over a year. That was the last job before I came back to Chicago to go into the Blue Room. But, anyway, I'm getting way ahead.
Yeah, let's get back to the --

Yeah, getting back to those early times in New York, you had to sweat and strain to make it. Eventually, -- almost immediately, on of the jazz affiononados who discovered me was Dan aley. And Dan aley was putting out records. Everybody was doing something. Gene Williams and Ralph Gleason, just out of Columbia University, were running

jazz information. There was another magazine called Jazz -- I can't think of it -- the Record Changer. That was in vogue. And they were more interested in discovering who was doing what on what record, and on what serial number and so forth on it, like a discography.

And Jazz Information also, but Jazz Information was also doing these articles, yes, and news. Then here comes Dan Whaley, with his solo art label. Solo Art was -- at that time he had recorded four black pianists, Cripple Clarence Lofton, Jimmy Yancey, Pete Johnson, Albert Ammons, I think, and maybe . But they all had been on his label, and now he wanted to record George Zach, and this is the story of how I happened -- no, Dan decided to give me a date. No, that's -- I'm almost mixed up. He gave me a date before Zach.

And I made South Side Shuffle and Ross Tavern Boogie because everybody -- by that time, the jazz people were hanging around Ross Tavern all the time. I can't think -- this fellow Brooks was singing every now and then and hanging around, and it was really a small group, and that was the big hangout. Every once in a while, Jimmy Ross would send a beer down, and it was a dismal basement. The water bugs were yay long, as big as your thumb, and there was a cat that would chase them around. And that was part of their floor show.
But we seemed to like coming down there and just

listening to the music. So I had a place to play. And Dan recorded me, and so now I was beginning to get more known. I wasn't living up to those expectations that I was going to tear the town apart, no tearing it apart, but I was getting more known especially with the collectors. As Leonard would say, I'd become the darling of the record collectors.

So eventually, I got a crack at something else. I worked in the Village at the Pirate's Den, as a solo. And about then, Zack came to New York, George Zack. And the boss at the Pirate's Den was very fascinated with him. And he just dreamt about having the two of us. But if you know something about George Zack, George liked to drink. And when he started to drink, nothing else mattered much. He wasn't ugly or vicious or fighting or anything. He just liked to drink and get into sort of a numb feeling.

And so the story that I got was, some boss brought George to New York, and this boss owned a hotel, some sort of hotel. And he said, George, I just want you to play this big dining room and I'm going to get you dressed up and everything so you'll feel at home. And he sent for the tailor -- got him a room, sent for the tailor, had him measured, got him something to eat, did everything that he should do, and then made one mistake.
He says, I got to go now, but if there's anything you need, just pick up the phone. Well, the gig never opened.

George called room service. And the booze came up and George was in seventh heaven. And he just sat there and drank, and whoever he knew in New York he called and they came up and joined him. It was just one party, and the boss couldn't stand that. He was going nowhere.

There was a later story about the -- George Hafer who ran that 'Hot Box' in DownBeat told me about, walking around in Chicago and a record shop, and some boss recognized him, says, you're George Hafer, aren't you? You write that 'Hot Box?' He says, yeah. He says, I read it, and you said something about piano players. Now, I'm really looking to find a piano player, and I need him for my place out there, in Lyons, Illinois.

And George says, wait a second, I write about these people but I don't want to recommend them. Boss says, don't worry about it, just tell me a good one and you're not in trouble, it's not your headache. So he says, well, George Zack is around and available. Well, now, about ten days later, George Hafer decides to go out to this place to see what's happening, see how it's -- because he hasn't heard a word.

And he goes out there at night, and this is what he sees. As he walks in the boss sees him and grabs him. He says, Mr. Hafer, come in here. Is this the way it's supposed to be? And Zack is sitting on the floor, reaching up for the keys, feeling no pain. And Zack had just made another -- but this was another one of the things that did not work out in
that period in New York. So I played the Pirate's Den alone and I played a few of the jobs. I got my union card.
As a soloist.
As a soloist. And then I got an offer from an agent who -- Freddy Williamson, who was second to Joe Glaser. But at that time he was working for another agency in New York.

And somehow, he had given me a few things to do at Downbeat. We had met and he had given me a few things. And he called me and asked me if I'd like to take a band into the Child's Fifth Avenue, 103rd and Broadway. And he said, --
Child's, was that like a cafeteria?

That was a cafeteria, and this was 1940. I'd been in New York practically two years, and so I said, sure. He says, okay, who would you like to have? I says, well, I'd like to have George Brunis who's available, I'd like to have Rod Clers Ron -- less. I don't know who I can get on drums. It turned out we got Joe Grasso. And on trumpet, I couldn't get Marty Marsala : he wasn't available. And I didn't know about I never I hadn't felt that scene yet.

And although we had one union in New York, there was no two unions, one for blacks and one for whites. But one union. But I hadn't really -- it was almost like I was numb to that happening. And so we made three leaders out of

it. We called it the Art Hodes Columbia Quintet, featuring Rod Cless Ron Cless and George Brunis and we also -- the three of us split the money. So the three leaders were getting $42.50 apiece and the two side men, $35. It was a big deal.

Now, we came to work, they had all sorts of business there during the daytime. And the manager said to him -- told us, says, now, I don't care what you do at 9:00, or 10:00 when you start playing. And he was very explicit. He says, you can even shit on the floor, if it'll do business. But you play a set from 7:00 to 9:00.
Two hour set.

Two hour set. Not continuous. We have people that come in here who have come here for years. We weigh out their food, and he pointed to this little white scale, for calories. And we don't want them disturbed. So whatever you do has to be nice and easy for them.

Now, if you can imagine George Brunis operating the lights. He hasn't had a drink yet that night, playing the chachas with the sticks or with the maracas, whatever it is, and Ron Cless doing the same, and everybody is waiting for that first drink which will happen at 10:00. We're making this scene very sober, right on the ground, and playing the waltzes, changing the lights so that the blue light comes in and the red light and the globe goes around and everything. So that we don't drive these people out.

But meanwhile, none of the None of them are coming in. None. None of them are coming in. They're waiting for 10:00 to come in. At 10:00, -- 9:00 we're through, we got one hour, we got lockers downstairs. Well, by that time, that's lunchtime, if you know what I mean.
