Everybody has got his own little taste in his own locker, and we're all ready. And you go down there and you get all ready and you relax and you forget about those two hours you just had.

And you're ready. And you come up there and you hit Muskrat or whatever you want to play, and the house is full. Because Gleason and Williams, because they'd been to Columbia and knew that scene, got me a tremendous writeup in the magazine there, and we had all those college kids coming in. Columbia was next door -- to hear this. And what the management did not know was -- or didn't seem to know, although it was their place, was that although they come in through the front door, there was no trick at all for them to go out through the side door, which was not monitored.
Oh, without paying.

Yes. So you're packing the place, -- and we don't know that he's not making it, because all we can see is how good we're doing. Wow, look at the people. They don't see the register. And so the job only lasted ten weeks. Again I'm getting ahead of myself.
Well, who was trumpet player at
We got -- I can't remember his name, he was a non-name. We had several.
How about the record that you did?
I can't remember.
Was that on your own label?

We put that out eventually -- well, here's what happened. We did not record for a label. Joe Grasso had a disc recorder of some sort. One of those ancient ones. And he brought that in one night and kept it by his drums. And while he was playing drums, he would operate this thing. And you know how much drums you can play and take care of a tape at the same time. It's quite a job. Today you do it and set it up and forget it until the end of the set. But then he was -- I think it was coming out on wire or something, a spool. I'm not sure.
It might have been an early wire recorder.

Whatever it was, he got it down and did get it on some discs, on some playbacks. And this is what came out, with noise and all, on the jazz record label eventually, which will not come out, I understand, on George Buck's label. He's finally going to reissue that, the whole series that we did for jazz records, everything that was --
Rod Less?
All the blues, everything.
Yeah, but that was -- the Blues Three was Bob Fields. And I didn't --
Right, he did some things with Benny Goodman.

Yeah. That was Cecil Scott later. All this was coming out. So here we are, knocking ourselves out knocking the audience out, having a ball there, with the night-time session. And then one day I made one of those mistakes musicians make every once in a while. Let's come down early and have some pictures taken. And as any musician knows, there goes the gig. The minute you take pictures or buy uniforms, that's the end of the gig. It's happened so many times with musicians. It's getting to be a law. Don't do it.

Well, we did, we came down. And that afternoon, we came down, we decided all to rehearse and get some new tunes.
that's another mistake.

That's the time the owner grabbed us and says, take two. What do you mean, take two? Take two weeks to find a new job, because we're through. Because here's the books, you're not doing it.

I says, you have to be kidding, this place is packed every night. He says, I don't know, it don't show on the

register. And I found out that what was happening, the kids were using that side door and ducking out. They'd have their drinks and food, they're gone. And nobody was monitoring the side door. I was completely unaware. I found out later. So you're out of work.
When was this?

This was 1940 and in Downbeat, I think there's a story there, some sort of square band and learn to eat regular and all that. And actually, Freddy Williamson did get me a job at a place in the Village, and again, I can't think of the name of it.

And the band was just like I said it would be. They dressed nice, they were neat, they were attentive, they came to work on time. They did everything right. And to such an extent that Freddy Williamson and I would use every intermission by going up to the floor above, which was sort of like a -- oh, a warehouse, almost, floor, nothing there but a pile of stuff. But it did have a piano and a dumbwaiter. And we'd just call down on the dumbwaiter and sent up a bunch of drinks. And we'd just sit there and I'd drink and get kind of knocked out and Freddy would sit there and get kind of knocked out. And I'd play. That was where I enjoyed myself.
Then I'd come down and perform. It was just one of those things. We'd play very innocuous music. We didn't hurt nobody. Everybody loved us, they liked us, we could have
stayed there for ages, except that I couldn't take it eventually. And the tuxedo and the whole thing. I was, like, in a cast, and I don't mean on the stage.
So but it lasted, I made enough money to pay a few bills, move into the Village, get a few sticks of furniture and the necessities of life.
And Thelma was back.

And -- yeah, she came back. She decided three months was enough, doing this and that. Somehow she'll build a fire under me and we'll do it together. And of course that's been the story of my life with her because she has, one way or another. (Inaudible.) There was a time when music was so bad I wanted to get out and sell pianos because I had an offer.
I remember that.
And she says, don't do it. Music has been too good to us. Don't do it.

Yeah, and it got very -- well, you know how this business can get, very horrible. Til you have no work, or distressing jobs. And if you can't do anything, if you can't do anything, then you're in trouble.
at that same time Ira Sullivan was selling clothes at some men's shop in I think
Oh, yeah.
You were talking about selling pianos and --

Yeah, I didn't volunteer, but I was teaching. And one day I looked at my hands and I says, well, you might as well give them away. They're not doing anything good. And well, that's an idea, why don't you teach? You can do that if you can't find jobs. You can teach, you might as well do something with them. And I started to teach. I got up to where I got about 40 pupils before I got sick of teaching, because I realized what I was doing was waiting for a lunch break or waiting for a smoke break or waiting for a coffee break, that I had too many people, I couldn't get interested in that many. It was more of an accumulation, of making a living out of it. So today, when I teach, I might have four people in a week. And I know each one of them, and I can say I'm going away to work, because this is not work, this is like gardening. Although you pay me, it's still like gardening, and I want to keep it that way. But then, it was a different matter. But, anyway, getting back to New York, I did do some accidental teaching in New York, because always somebody came along and says, you play so simple in effect, is what they said to me. And I think you could teach me how to play. And I would say, if you

can whistle, I can teach you how to play the blues. You want to play the blues? If you can whistle, you can hear a note, I can show you with one finger, I can show you a bass. And we'll sit down and have some fun.

Man, I got some of the darndest people -- you know, one at a time, one today, one next year, who'd insist on making good on their promises. But those were the early years. By now I'm getting acquainted with Eddie Condon, is in town and I've sat in at Nick's, and all this bumping heads and breaking ground. And I've played at Jimmy Ryan's.

The big thing, to be heard by your peers. It was so important. They had a jam session at Jimmy Ryan's that was run by Eddie Condon and Milt Gabler. Now, Eddie didn't do too much running, he sat on the -- he was either at the bar or he was onstage, pointing his finger, you've got the next chorus, something like that. But behind the scenes, Eddie was a tremendous worker. And and his work was out of the place, digging up things to do.

A story about Eddie that very few people know is that one time there was 18 newspapermen -- I may be exaggerating -- at Nick's to hear the band that he was in, and he picked up the check for every one of them.
Well, he got very good press.
That was why. He was very aware. And his wife was a copywriter for Life or Look or something. She
knew press. And then his brother-in-law, he had the right connections. And whatever his name was, the press agent.
Anderson.

Yeah, Ernie Anderson loved him, just like Milt Gabler loved him. So they made a lot of things possible. So here's this jam session. All I have to do is wait for Earl Hines to step down, some Sunday, Fats Waller, Jimmy Johnson, Joe Sullivan, and then maybe I'll be next. And then here comes Joe Bushkin, where did he come from?
But finally, somebody's pushing and I finally get called up to play, the big moment. Just to sit in.
You had to stand in line.

Stand in line, just to sit in. And let me tell you something about drummers that you might be surprised to hear. We have a fellow by the name of Kansas around Chicago. And he supposedly was a tremendous drummer. Now, in those days, like I say, drums was not breaking it up and all that nonsense. And I'm onstage with Sidney Bechet. And somehow the drummer took the chorus, and when it got done it wasn't like when we started. We were a little -- the 32 bars were either 30 or 34, something had happened.

And I'm outside, and Sidney Bechet is eating his rear end out about how to do this, what to do about playing music. Not telling him to hold the sticks or anything, just about the musical part, because drummers then -- there was a
different scene. You got more bars maybe to take a break, but you weren't taking a whole chorus.
Yeah. And very few people -- now when they give the drummer a course, it seems to me that they just want to rest for a while.
Sid Catlett was the first one that impressed me as being so musical, you could hear the changes in the tune.

That he could do it. Very few can do it today, in my opinion, again. But anyway, I'm finally at Rind's and I'm finally invited to play, one Sunday afternoon. It wasn't a big deal. I think I paid either seven or ten dollars. I remember playing City College and I hired Eddie Condon, Mezz Crow, Cliff Jackson, Frankie Newton and Dave Tough at seven dollars apiece, on Collins Stage, and I got ten for being leader and getting them together.

This was money in those days. You could still hire most musicians up til '46, say, '47, for a paltry -- Nick's paid no more than $40 a week. If you could get your money. Many times the guys waited weeks or -- for their money, they're always behind, oh, yes.
That's startling because of the publicity about Nick's. Known all over the world and the guys that played there become --

Salaries were very meager to my knowledge. They never got big. Well, it's surprising when you talk to today and find out that Jimmy Ryan's pays a fat $25 a side man a night? And when you go to buy a drink at Jimmy Ryan's, what does it cost you, $2.75, $2.50? And that's the scale? A six night week gets you a fat -- that's why Herbie Hall has retired to Bourne, Texas. He's living there, but he will take jobs. But he doesn't -- there's nothing there in town.
Yeah, I know, New York is still Scuffle City.

And the other fat job, Eddie Condon's, pays $35 a night. Now, that's what he just told us, and he lives there. I mean, this is the big deal of being -- and yet, if you're called a New Yorker, -- and I've had that, to call this clarinet player, Joe M . ., to go on the road when Willie Dorsett got sick on the tour, and couldn't make it in Greenwich, Connecticut, I called Joe M . And we're talking about $500 a week. Couldn't budget him. Got that New York address, you know.
Early '40s for me was quite a financial struggle. If you got lucky enough to get a job for $35 a week, you could do a lot of things with that $35. We furnished our apartment and --
You lived in the Village?

We lived down in the Village, and the jazz record office became -- what they used for an office, in Tenth Street, was right -- the basement below -- store basement below where we lived, it was right down there.
Well, --
You had a record date in -- was it 1940 that you were telling me about the record date?
Yeah. The first record date was for Dan Whaley.
The solo.
Solo. And the next ones was -- I'd met Rod Gless. Of course, we played Columbia Quintet.
You knew Rod in Chicago?
I knew Rod in Chicago, but now we got rather thick. And so -- and Bob Thiele was his man. Bob thought Rod was the greatest.

And so he decided to record on this jazz label. And Rod had gotten me and there was going to be a trio, and he got this Jimmy , bass player. And so we made a record for Bob Thiele. Now, it was after that that Don alely decided to record George Zack. And again, the story, he's got George all ready, he stayed with him the night before, he's just glued to him. And now they're in Ross' Tavern, or some tavern, having a drink, because George has to have atmosphere, he can't go up there in that cold studio. And he says, okay,

tell you what, we'll have three drinks, and then we go, okay? George says, okay, that'll be fine. So they had the first, they had the second, they order the third, and aley says, I'm going to the phone to call the studio and tell them that we're coming. George says, that's fine.
And he went to the phone. And when he got back, it wasn't fine, it was too late, because George had called the bartender and said, don't spare the horses.
And that's why I got to make selections from the gutter, the blues, because --

Yeah, well, Commodore got the tape. It was done -- either -- I'm not sure if it was solo art or - yes, solo art did it. Theal had something to do with it, I don't know, maybe picking up the tab or something. I seem to feel his presence somewhere behind there, but I can't pinpoint it. My memory does not serve me that well, as regards that.

But I did get that date because of George not being able to make it. And the time was paid for, the studio was paid for. And I was ready. They called me, I came in and I made ten three-minute tunes. And I still got the tracks at home somewhere. I'm not crazy about many of them. But Selections from the Gutter was one of them.
Were all of them issued?
No, no. But I've got the test pressing. And they're all marked down in the discography that Ro Fairchild put out a small discography on me, and he knows about it, so it's in there.

So that's how I got to play. Now, it was these little things that start getting you publicity if you're little known. The story of -- that I've never told anyone, I don't know, but I just got through writing it for this book that Jan Hansen and I are putting out together. This story was -- I'm now at Jimmy Ryan's with my old trio. I've got Damy Alvinn anyhow, my own trio, finally. And somebody comes in and says, you got a writeup in Cue magazine.

Wow. I run out for blocks until I could find Cue, and I dig the copy, and now I'm back to work. And I'm waiting for the job to happen, because I'm not even going to look at it yet, I'm going to take my time. So I got this writeup and if you ever remember Cue magazine --
Vaguely.

Well, it's like the New Yorker, it has -- mostly for music. But the type in the New Yorker is large enough that you don't need glasses. The type in Cue was very small, very -- you had to almost glare at it at a short distance.
Now, it was after work, I found a restuarant that's

open, a one-armed joint, and I'm sitting at the counter and I order the -- I'm a little stoned, I've been working all night. And I'm sitting there looking at that writeup, it says, Art Hodes and his trio have opened at Jimmy Ryan's at 52nd Street. And he's featuring Danny Alvin and Mezzrow, real good music.

And I'm reading it and reading it and reading it. I must have -- I don't know how long I'm in there. I must have been there at least 45 minutes. And suddenly the place is swarming with police. And it seems that while I was reading this writeup, some character -- and I heard somebody come in, came and sat way down at the end of the counter, got something to eat and as he walked out to pay the bill, there were some billboards between the cash register and the window. So that the outside people couldn't see in so good. He got a gun and held a man up.
While you were sitting there.
While I was sitting there, looking at this writeup.
Okay.

Now, you can believe these cops, how they bought my story. When they saw the size of the writeup, and they looked at me out of the side of their eye, and the only thing that saved me is Jimmy Ryan. I woke up Jimmy Ryan and he woke up and came and came down there and identified me. And they still figured I ought to get locked up.
But they let me go. They believed me then that I hadn't seen anything. And I never saw the guy, I don't know what he looked like. But this was one of my first writeups.

This is how impressed you get, when you make the New York scene. That's it. So these were the early struggles in New York, until you start getting a few other breaks. Village Vanguard was a break. You go in there with your own trio, and I went in there with Max Kaminsky and Freddy , and then I came back or either extended the engagement when Max had left with Wild Bill Davison and Freddy , working off as the group -- the Lion of Trinidad, who was a calypso innovator, and writer. He wrote that tune, never marry a woman prettier than you if you want to be happy and have a good life, always pick an ugly woman for your wife.

So he was there. Pearl Bailey -- I saw Pearl Bailey on that floor, she was making either $40 or $75 a week. And Max Gordon, the big impresario, standing in the back with me, saying, I don't know what's wrong with that gal, there's something I can quite figure out. You know what he figured out? He bought the Blue Angel on the East Side with a partner, and within a couple of years, he's paying Pearl Bailey $1500 a week, and she hasn't changed a bit of that act. That's what he figured out.
She came in doing the same act. He just didn't understand it. For $75 a week, he couldn't understand it.

For $1500, he thought -- this is what tickles me about people that know. Pearl was a natural, she knocked me out, getting out in the middle of the floor, doing, It's a Long Way to Tipperary. And she had a way of -- like, her brother was a great dancer. Her hands would keep a beat, her little palm, she palmed the beat with her hands. And it was just a pleasure to play for her and watch her.
So those were the kind of people that were in the Vanguard.
Did Bruzey work at the --

He worked also as an act, and that's where Big Bill -- I always remember, Big Bill Broonzy and Wild Bill Davison and going out and getting a fifth of booze, of some kind of whiskey. And Wild Bill had a drink and then Big Bill grabbed the bottle. And when he got through putting it down behind -- from his mouth, I could see where the bottom of his fist was, the whiskey was below that bottom. And I says, no more, I ain't going in with him in no bottles no more.

But he was a real warm character, and he was a great player. I think he was so underestimated, but if you happened to hear the recording of him playing by himself on guitar and see what he could do with a guitar and how many tunes he wrote, just the most obvious, When You're White You're All Right, When You're Brown Stick Around, and When You're
Black Get In The Back, way back, things like that. But that was a protest. But he wrote blues, too. I forget all of them. But he was really something to work for.
So all this was happening at the Vanguard. Next was down the block and across the street. The Village was jumping.
Was there a place called the Pied Piper down there?
And the Pied Piper was around the corner from the Pirate's Den, and that's where Max Kaminsky wound up having a band. And now we're talking about '46 -- '45, '46, it's getting late.
But while I'm down at -- sometime while I'm either at the Vanguard or at Nyon's, but in that early period, the jazz boys grabbed me again. And this time, it's --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

And on the way, Pee Wee says, I know a man. I says, let's stop in, so we stopped in to see him. And he had a bar, it was the Back Room. And there was nothing happening in the Back Room. So Pee Wee says, how about letting us have the Back Room? And the boss says, fine, it's yours, go ahead and do whatever you want with it.

So he put up a sign above his awning, Pee Wee and Art's Back Room. And within the end of the week, he gave us $30 a week apiece, advance. Meanwhile, we were hiring a bass player, Herb Ward, at $75 a week. So we'd have a trio. At least, two would play and then Pee Wee would come in and so forth. So anyway, we lasted over a year, and then that whole year we booked Jack Teagarden with his band -- Louis Armstrong was having his teeth taken out or fixed and the band was laid off. Jack did a week, did eight days there. And that was a real --
I never knew that, I . . . never read anything about it.

Almost immediately we got Chippy Hill to come and sing. And then we got Willie the Lion Smith. So we had Willie the Lion Smith playing opposite me. As Bonny Bigarde says when he came in there, I like to come in there and see you two guys bumping heads. I never thought I was doing any bumping of heads, because I was in awe of Willie. And I sat there and listened to him play, and every key in the piano he could start a tune.

And there was a trumpet player would come in, an Italian fellow, that we called Face, because of his face, the look on his face, the -- whatever God gave him as a face, it was something different. But Face wanted to play trumpet. And Willie was most kind. Willie could only take so much. So pretty soon Willie would start changing keys, and Face couldn't make that.

But otherwise, Willie would say, okay, boy, go out and get me some cigars, and give him some money and get rid of him. But Willie was an education, just listening to them play, he was a real tremendous stride pianist that knew so many tunes, he was a composer, too, and I didn't think I was bumping any heads with this one. And Pee Wee and I played together and then I played with the bass player, opposite Willie.
Now, we lasted there over a year. That was the last job before I came back to Chicago to go into the Blue Note. But, anyway, I'm getting way ahead.
Yeah, let's get back to the --

Yeah, getting back to those early times in New York, you had to sweat and strain to make it. Eventually, -- almost immediately, on of the jazz affionados who discovered me was Dan Qualey. And Dan Qualey was putting out records. Everybody was doing something. Gene Williams and Ralph Gleason, just out of Columbia University, were running

Jazz Information. There was another magazine called Jazz -- I can't think of it -- the Record Changer. That was in vogue. And they were more interested in discovering who was doing what on what record, and on what serial number and so forth on it, like a discography.

And Jazz Information also, but Jazz Information was also doing these articles, yes, and news. Then here comes Dan Qualey, with his Solo Art label. Solo Art was -- at that time he had recorded four black pianists, Cripple Clarence Loften, Jimmy Yancy, Pete Johnson, Albert Ammons, I think, and maybe Meade Lux Lewis. But they all had been on his label, and now he wanted to record George Zack, and this is the story of how I happened -- no, Dan decided to give me a date. No, that's -- I'm almost mixed up. He gave me a date before Zach.

And I made 'South Side Shuffle' and 'Ross Tavern Boogie' because everybody -- by that time, the jazz people were hanging around Ross Tavern all the time. I can't think -- this fellow Brooks was singing every now and then and hanging around, and it was really a small group, and that was the big hangout. Every once in a while, Jimmy Ross would send a beer down, and it was a dismal basement. The water bugs were yay long, as big as your thumb, and there was a cat that would chase them around. And that was part of their floor show.
But we seemed to like coming down there and just

listening to the music. So I had a place to play. And Dan recorded me, and so now I was beginning to get more known. I wasn't living up to those expectations that I was going to tear the town apart, no tearing it apart, but I was getting more known especially with the collectors. As Leonard would say, I'd become the darling of the record collectors.

So eventually, I got a crack at something else. I worked in the Village at the Pirate's Den, as a solo. And about then, Zack came to New York, George Zack. And the boss at the Pirate's Den was very fascinated with him. And he just dreamt about having the two of us. But if you know something about George Zack, George liked to drink. And when he started to drink, nothing else mattered much. He wasn't ugly or vicious or fighting or anything. He just liked to drink and get into sort of a numb feeling.

And so the story that I got was, some boss brought George to New York, and this boss owned a hotel, some sort of hotel. And he said, George, I just want you to play this in big dining room and I'm going to get you dressed up and everything so you'll feel at home. And he sent for the tailor -- got him a room, sent for the tailor, had him measured, got him something to eat, did everything that he should do, and then made one mistake.
He says, I got to go now, but if there's anything you need, just pick up the phone. Well, the gig never opened.

George called room service. And the booze came up and George was in seventh heaven. And he just sat there and drank, and whoever he knew in New York he called and they came up and joined him. It was just one party, and the boss couldn't stand that. He was going nowhere.

There was a later story about the -- George Haefer who ran that "Hot Box" in DownBeat told me about, walking around in Chicago and a record shop, and some boss recognized him, says, you're George Haefer, aren't you? You write that "Hot Box?" He says, yeah. He says, I read it, and you said something about piano players. Now, I'm really looking to find a piano player, and I need him for my place out there, in Lyons, Illinois.

And George says, wait a second, I write about these people but I don't want to recommend them. Boss says, don't worry about it, just tell me a good one and you're not in trouble, it's not your headache. So he says, well, George Zach is around and available. Well, now, about ten days later, George Haefer decides to go out to this place to see what's happening, see how it's -- because he hasn't heard a word.

And he goes out there at night, and this is what he sees. As he walks in the boss sees him and grabs him. He says, Mr. Haefer, come in here. Is this the way it's supposed to be? And Zack is sitting on the floor, reaching up for the keys, feeling no pain. And Zack had just made another -- but this was another one of the things that did not work out in
that period in New York. So I played the Pirate's Den alone and I played a few of the jobs. I got my union card.
As a soloist.
As a soloist. And then I got an offer from an agent who -- Freddy Williamson, who was second to Joe Glaser. But at that time he was working for another agency in New York.

And somehow, he had given me a few things to do at DownBeat. We had met and he had given me a few things. And he called me and asked me if I'd like to take a band into the Childe's Fifth Avenue, 103rd and Broadway. And he said, --
Childe's, was that like a cafeteria?

That was a cafeteria, and this was 1940. I'd been in New York practically two years, and so I said, sure. He says, okay, who would you like to have? I says, well, I'd like to have George Brunis who's available, I'd like to have Rod Cless. I don't know who I can get on drums. It turned out we got Joe Grasso. And on trumpet, I couldn't get Marty Marsala, he wasn't available. And I didn't know about experience. I never had one yet. I hadn't felt that scene yet.

And although we had one union in New York, there was no two unions, one for blacks and one for whites. But one union. But I hadn't really -- it was almost like I was numb to that happening. And so we made three leaders out of

it. We called it the Art Hodes Columbia Quintet, featuring Rod Kless and George Brunis and we also -- the three of us split the money. So the three leaders were getting $42.50 apiece and the two side men, $35. It was a big deal.

Now, we came to work, they had all sorts of business there during the daytime. And the marager said to him -- told us, says, now, I don't care what you do at 9:00, or 10:00 when you start playing. And he was very explicit. He says, you can even shit on the floor, if it'll do business. But you play a set from 7:00 to 9:00.
Two hour set.

Two hour set. Not continuous. We have people that come in here who have come here for years. We weigh out their food, and he pointed to this little white scale, for calories. And we don't want them disturbed. So whatever you do has to be nice and easy for them.

Now, if you can imagine George Brunis operating the lights. He hasn't had a drink yet that night, playing the chachas with the sticks or with the maracas, whatever it is, and Rod Kless doing the same, and everybody is waiting for that first drink which will happen at 10:00. We're making this scene very sober, right on the ground, and playing the waltzes, changing the lights so that the blue light comes in and the red light and the globe goes around and everything. So that we don't drive these people out.

But meanwhile, none of the jazz people - None of them are coming in. None. None of them are coming in. They're waiting for 10:00 to come in. At 10:00, -- 9:00 we're through, we got one hour, we got lockers downstairs. Well, by that time, that's lunchtime, if you know what I mean. Everybody has got his own little taste in his own locker, and we're all ready. And you go down there and you get all ready and you relax and you forget about those two hours you just had.

And you're ready. And you come up there and you hit Muskrat or whatever you want to play, and the house is full. Because Gleason and Williams, because they'd been to Columbia and knew that scene, got me a tremendous writeup in the magazine there, and we had all those college kids coming in. Columbia was next door -- to hear this. And what the management did not know was -- or didn't seem to know, although it was their place, was that although they come in through the front door, there was no trick at all for them to go out through the side door, which was not monitored.
Oh, without paying.

Yes. So you're packing the place, -- and we don't know that he's not making it, because all we can see is how good we're doing. Wow, look at the people. They don't see the register. And so the job only lasted ten weeks. Again I'm getting ahead of myself.
Well, who was trumpet player at
that time?
We got -- I can't remember his name, he was a non-name. We had several.
How about the record that you did?
I can't remember.
Was that on your own label?

We put that out eventually -- well, here's what happened. We did not record for a label. Joe Grasso had a disc recorder of some sort. One of those ancient ones. And he brought that in one night and kept it by his drums. And while he was playing drums, he would operate this thing. And you know how much drums you can play and take care of a tape at the same time. It's quite a job. Today you do it and set it up and forget it until the end of the set. But then he was -- I think it was coming out on wire or something, a spool. I'm not sure.
It might have been an early wire recorder.

Whatever it was, he got it down and did get it on some discs, on some playbacks. And this is what came out, with noise and all, on the jazz record label eventually, which will now come out, I understand, on George Buck's label. He's finally going to reissue that, the whole series that we did for jazz records, everything that was -- stuff with
Including the Rod Cless?
All the blues, everything.
The Blues Three
Yeah, but that was -- the Blues Three was Bob Thiele. And I didn't --
Right, he did some things with Henry Goodwin.

Yeah. That was Cecil Scott later. All this was coming out. So here we are, knocking ourselves out knocking the audience out, having a ball there, with the night-time session. And then one day I made one of those mistakes musicians make every once in a while. Let's come down early and have some pictures taken. And as any musician knows, there goes the gig. The minute you take pictures or buy uniforms, that's the end of the gig. It's happened so many times with musicians. It's getting to be a law. Don't do it. Well, we did, we came down. And that afternoon, we came down, we decided all to rehearse and get some new tunes.
that's another mistake.

That's the time the owner grabbed us and says, take two. What do you mean, take two? Take two weeks to find a new job, because we're through. Because here's the books, you're not doing it. I says, you have to be kidding, this place is packed every night. He says, I don't know, it don't show on the

register. And I found out that what was happening, the kids were using that side door and ducking out. They'd have their drinks and food, they're gone. And nobody was monitoring the side door. I was completely unaware. I found out later. So you're out of work.
When was this?

This was 1940 and in DownBeat, I think there's a story there, I'm just going to get some sort of square band and learn to eat regular and all that. And actually, Freddy Williamson did get me a job at a place in the Village, and again, I can't think of the name of it.

And the band was just like I said it would be. They dressed nice, they were neat, they were attentive, they came to work on time. They did everything right. And to such an extent that Freddy Williamson and I would use every intermission by going up to the floor above, which was sort of like a -- oh, a warehouse, almost, floor, nothing there but a pile of stuff. But it did have a piano and a dumbwaiter. And we'd just call down on the dumbwaiter and sent up a bunch of drinks. And we'd just sit there and I'd drink and get kind of knocked out and Freddy would sit there and get kind of knocked out. And I'd play. That was where I enjoyed myself.
Then I'd come down and perform. It was just one of those things. We'd play very innocuous music. We didn't hurt nobody. Everybody loved us, they liked us, we could have
stayed there for ages, except that I couldn't take it eventually. And the tuxedo and the whole thing. I was, like, in a cast, and I don't mean on the stage.
So but it lasted, I made enough money to pay a few bills, move into the Village, get a few sticks of furniture and the necessities of life.
And Thelma was back.

And -- yeah, she came back. She decided three months was enough, doing this and that. Somehow she'll build a fire under me and we'll do it together. And of course that's been the story of my life with her because she has, one way or another. Worked in my corner to animate me. There was a time when music was so bad I wanted to get out and sell pianos because I had an offer.
I remember that.
And she says, don't do it. Music has been too good to us. Don't do it.
That was around 1960.

Yeah, and it got very -- well, you know how this business can get, very horrible. Til you have no work, or distressing jobs. And if you can't do anything, if you can't do anything, then you're in trouble.
That's -- at that same time Ira Sullivan was selling clothes at some men's shop in I think Rothschilds in Park Forest.
Oh, yeah.
You were talking about selling pianos and --

Yeah, I didn't volunteer, but I was teaching. And one day I looked at my hands and I says, well, you might as well give them away. They're not doing anything good. And the says, well, that's an idea, why don't you teach? You can do that if you can't find jobs. You can teach, you might as well do something with them.

And I started to teach. I got up to where I got about 40 pupils before I got sick of teaching, because I realized what I was doing was waiting for a lunch break or waiting for a smoke break or waiting for a coffee break, that I had too many people, I couldn't get interested in that many. It was more of an accumulation, of making a living out of it. And thats a different thing. So today, when I teach, I might have four people in a week. And I know each one of them, and I can say I'm going away to work, because this is not work, this is like gardening. Although you pay me, it's still like gardening, and I want to keep it that way.

But then, it was a different matter. But, anyway, getting back to New York, I did do some accidental teaching in New York, because always somebody came along and says, you play so simple in effect, is what they said to me. And I think you could teach me how to play. And I would say, if you

can whistle, I can teach you how to play the blues. You want to play the blues? If you can whistle, you can hear a note, I can show you with one finger, I can show you a bass. And we'll sit down and have some fun.

Man, I got some of the darndest people -- you know, one at a time, one today, one next year, who'd insist on making good on their promises. But those were the early years. By now I'm getting acquainted with Eddie Condon, Muggsy Spanier is in town and I've sat in at Nick's, and all this bumping heads and breaking ground. And I've played at Jimmy Ryan's.

The big thing, to be heard by your peers. It was so important. They had a jam session at Jimmy Ryan's that was run by Eddie Condon and Milt Gabler. Now, Eddie didn't do too much running, he sat on the -- he was either at the bar or he was onstage, pointing his finger, you've got the next course, something like that. But behind the scenes, Eddie was a tremendous worker. And best mind, and his work was out of the place, digging up things to do.

A story about Eddie that very few people know is that one time there was 18 newspapermen -- I may be exaggerating -- at Nick's to hear the band that he was in, and he picked up the check for every one of them.
Well, he got very good press.
That was why. He was very aware. And his wife was a copyrighter for Life or Look or something. She
knew press. And then his brother-in-law, he had the right connections. And whatever his name was, the press agent that was in his corner.
Anderson.

Yeah, Ernie Anderson loved him, just like Milt Gabler loved him. So they made a lot of things possible. So here's this jam session. All I have to do is wait for Earl Hines to step down, some Sunday, Fats Waller, Jimmy Johnson, Joe Sullivan, and then maybe I'll be next. And then here comes Joe Bushkin, where did he come from?
But finally, somebody's pushing and I finally get called up to play, the big moment. Just to sit in.
You had to stand in line.

Stand in line, just to sit in. And let me tell you something about drummers that you might be surprised to hear. We have a fellow by the name of Kansas [Fields] around Chicago. And he supposedly was a tremendous drummer. Now, in those days, like I say, drums was not breaking it up and all that nonsense. And I'm onstage with Sidney Bechet. And somehow the drummer took the course, and when it got done it wasn't like when we started. We were a little -- the 32 bars were either 30 or 34, something had happened.

And now I'm outside, and Sidney Bechet is eating his rear end out about how to do this, what to do about playing music. Not telling him to hold the sticks or anything, just about the musical part, because drummers then -- there was a
different scene. You got more bars maybe to take a break, but you weren't taking a whole course.
You take certain lengths of time rather than a chorus.
Yeah. And very few people -- now when they give the drummer a course, it seems to me that they just want to rest for a while.
Sid Catlett was the first one that impressed me as being so musical, you could hear the changes in the tune.

That he could do it. Very few can do it today, in my opinion, again. But anyway, I'm finally at Rind's and I'm finally invited to play, one Sunday afternoon. It wasn't a big deal. I think I paid either seven or ten dollars. I remember playing City College and I hired Eddie Conlon, Mezzrow, Cliff Jackson, Frankie Newton and Davy Tough at seven dollars apiece, a college date, and I got ten for being leader and getting them together.

This was money in those days. You could still hire most musicians up til '46, say, '47, for a paltry -- Nick's paid no more than $40 a week. If you could get your money. Many times the guys waited weeks or -- for their money, they're always behind, oh, yes.
That's startling because of the publicity about Nick's. Known all over the world and the guys that played there become --

Salaries were very meager to my knowledge. They never got big. Well, it's surprising when you talk to Kenny Davern today and find out that Jimmy Ryan's pays a fat $25 a side man a night? And when you go to buy a drink at Jimmy Ryan's, what does it cost you, $2.75, $2.50? And that's the scale? A six night week gets you a fat -- that's why Herbie Hall has retired to Bourne, Texas. He's living there, but he will take jobs. But he doesn't -- there's nothing there in town.
Yeah, I know, New York is still Scuffle City.

And the other fat job, Eddie Condon's, pays $35 a night. Now, that's what he just told us, and he lives there. I mean, this is the big deal of being -- and yet, if you're called a New Yorker, -- and I've had that, to call this clarinet player, Joe Muranyi, to go on the road when Volly DeFaut got sick on the tour, and couldn't make it in Greenwich, Connecticut, I called Joe Muranyi. And we're talking about $500 a week. I couldn't budge him. Got that New York address, you know.
Early '40s for me was quite a financial struggle. If you got lucky enough to get a job for $35 a week, you could do a lot of things with that $35. We furnished our apartment and --
You lived in the Village?

We lived down in the Village, and the jazz record office became -- what they used for an office, in Tenth Street, was right -- the basement below -- store basement below where we lived, it was right down there.
Well, --
You had a record date in -- was it 1940 that you were telling me about the record date?
Yeah. The first record date was for Dan Qualey.
The solo.
Solo. And the next ones was -- I'd met Rod Cless. Of course, we played Columbia Quintet.
You knew Rod in Chicago?
I knew Rod in Chicago, but now we got rather thick. And so -- and Bob Thiele was his man. Bob Theal thought Rod was the greatest.

And so he decided to record on this jazz label. And Rod had gotten me and there was going to be a trio, and he got this Jimmy Butts, bass player. And so we made a record for Bob Thiele. Now, it was after that that Don Qualey decided to record George Zack. And again, the story, he's got George all ready, he stayed with him the night before, he's just glued to him. And now they're in Ross' Tavern, or some tavern, having a drink, because George has to have atmosphere, he can't go up there in that cold studio. And he says, okay,

tell you what, we'll have three drinks, and then we go, okay? George says, okay, that'll be fine. So they had the first, they had the second, they order the third, and Qualey says, I'm going to the phone to call the studio and tell them that we're coming. George says, that's fine.
And he went to the phone. And when he got back, it wasn't fine, it was too late, because George had called the bartender and said, don't spare the horses.
Booze has hurt so many musicians, especially from that era.
And that's why I got to make "Selections from the Gutter", the blues, because --
That was for Commodore, wasn't it?

Yeah, well, Commodore got the tape. It was done -- either -- I'm not sure if it was solo art or - yes, solo art did it. Theal had something to do with it, I don't know, maybe picking up the tab or something. I seem to feel his presence somewhere behind there, but I can't pinpoint it. My memory does not serve me that well, as regards that.

But I did get that date because of George not being able to make it. And the time was paid for, the studio was paid for. And I was ready. They called me, I came in and I made ten three-minute tunes. And I still got the tracks at home somewhere. I'm not crazy about many of them. But "Selections from the Gutter" was one of them.
Were all of them issued?

No, no. But I've got the test pressing. And they're all marked down in the discography that Rolfe Fairchild put out a small discography on me, and he knows about it, so it's in there.

So that's how I got to play. Now, it was these little things that start getting you publicity if you're little known. The story of -- that I've never told anyone, I don't know, but I just got through writing it for this book that Jan Hansen and I are putting out together. This story was I opened with Mezz and Danny -- I'm now at Jimmy Ryan's with my old trio. I've got -- I think Alvin; anyhow, my own trio, finally. And somebody comes in and says, you got a writeup in Cue magazine.

Wow. I run out for blocks until I could find Cue, and I dig the copy, and now I'm back to work. And I'm waiting for the job to happen, because I'm not even going to look at it yet, I'm going to take my time. So I got this writeup and if you ever remember Cue magazine --
Vaguely.

Well, it's like the New Yorker, it has -- mostly for music. But the type in the New Yorker is large enough that you don't need glasses. The type in Cue was very small, very -- you had to almost glare at it at a short distance.

Now, it was after work, I found a restuarant that's

open, a one-armed joint, and I'm sitting at the counter and I order the -- I'm a little stoned, I've been working all night. And I'm sitting there looking at that writeup, it says, Art Hodes and his trio have opened at Jimmy Ryan's at 52nd Street. And he's featuring Danny Alvin and Mezzrow, real good music.

And I'm reading it and reading it and reading it. I must have -- I don't know how long I'm in there. I must have been there at least 45 minutes. And suddenly the place is swarming with police. And it seems that while I was reading this writeup, some character -- and I heard somebody come in, came and sat way down at the end of the counter, got something to eat and as he walked out to pay the bill, there were some billboards between the cash register and the window. So that the outside people couldn't see in so good. He got a gun and held a man up.
While you were sitting there.
While I was sitting there, looking at this writeup.
Okay.

Now, you can believe these cops, how they bought my story. When they saw the size of the writeup, and they looked at me out of the side of their eye, and the only thing that saved me is Jimmy Ryan. I woke up Jimmy Ryan and he woke up and came and came down there and identified me. And they still figured I ought to get locked up.
But they let me go. They believed me then that I hadn't seen anything. And I never saw the guy, I don't know what he looked like. But this was one of my first writeups.

This is how impressed you get, when you make the New York scene. That's it. So these were the early struggles in New York, until you start getting a few other breaks. Village Vanguard was a break. You go in there with your own trio, and I went in there with Max Kaminsky and Freddy Moore and then I came back or either extended the engagement when Max had left with Wild Bill Davison and Freddy Moore, working off as the group -- the Lion of Trinidad, who was a calypso innovator, and writer. He wrote that tune, 'never marry a woman prettier than you if you want to be happy and have a good life, always pick an ugly woman for your wife.'

So he was there. Pearl Bailey -- I saw Pearl Bailey on that floor, she was making either $40 or $75 a week. And Max Gordon, the big impresario, standing in the back with me, saying, I don't know what's wrong with that gal, there's something I can quite figure out. You know what he figured out? He bought the Blue Angel on the East Side with a partner, and within a couple of years, he's paying Pearl Bailey $1500 a week, and she hasn't changed a bit of that act. That's what he figured out.
She came in doing the same act. He just didn't understand it. For $75 a week, he couldn't understand it.

For $1500, he thought -- this is what tickles me about people that know. Pearl was a natural, she knocked me out, getting out in the middle of the floor, doing, 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary.' And she had a way of -- like, her brother was a great dancer. Her hands would keep a beat, her little palm, she palmed the beat with her hands. And it was just a pleasure to play for her and watch her.
So those were the kind of people that were in the Vanguard.
Did Brownzy work at the --

He worked also as an act, and that's where Big Bill -- I always remember, Big Bill Brownzy and Wild Bill Davison and Art Hodes going out and getting a fifth of booze, of some kind of whiskey. And Wild Bill had a drink and then Big Bill grabbed the bottle. And when he got through putting it down behind -- from his mouth, I could see where the bottom of his fist was, the whiskey was below that bottom. And I says, no more, I ain't going in with him in no bottles no more.

But he was a real warm character, and he was a great player. I think he was so underestimated, but if you happened to hear the right recording of him playing by himself on guitar and see what he could do with a guitar and how many tunes he wrote, just the most obvious, 'When You're White You're All Right, When You're Brown Stick Around, and When You're
Black Get In The Back, way back, things like that. But that "Kingdom of the Highway," was a protest. But he wrote blues, too. I forget all of them. But he was really something to work for.
So all this was happening at the Vanguard. Next was down the block and across the street. The Village was jumping.
Was there a place called the Pied Piper down there?
And the Pied Piper was around the corner from the Pirate's Den, and that's where MLX Kaminisky wound up having a band. And now we're talking about '46 -- '45, '46, it's getting late.
But while I'm down at -- sometime while I'm either at the Vanguard or at Ryan's, but in that early period, the Jazz Information boys grabbed me again. And this time, it's --

Get that bum off the air, he's commercial. Now, I'm not getting a penny salary. I'm either buying my own records or they're being furnished to me. I'm paying my own carfare, I'm paying my own lunch. So there was no talking to the guy. The guy that was running the station, there was no way in the world you could talk to that little fire rat. So they just warned me, cool it, on the announcing. There was no way I could cool it. I didn't have no secretary, I was getting letters. I had an audience of a million kids or so, from around New York, New England.

What amazes me is, so many of those kids that were listening then still remember. I've seen it happen over and over again, in concerts and like this engagements. People come up and say, I used to listen to that.
I listened to that program. Pee Wee Russell --
It's converted a lot of people.

Yeah, and Pee Wee Russell told me, he stopped playing his records. He says, all I have -- I get up with your program, and I know I'm going to hear all the records I want to hear on your program. And this is the first time

Leonard Feather, the critic, and I fell apart. Because he came up to that station with Duke Ellington records. And I had a very narrow -- as honestly as I can be now -- approach to what I thought my role of promoting jazz was. I say narrow from the standpoint of where I sit now. It wasn't bad, I believed in it, I believe in it now. But it was very close. It had to be the Hot Five's, the Hot Seven's, Bessie Smith, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller -- that era of jazz.
And I loved Duke, I collected Duke. But I didn't think he needed my help, and I think that music did.
Leonard was working for Duke.
Leonard was working for Duke.
But he was also working as a critic.
Working as a critic. And this always later on disturbed me very much.
This is to me unethical. Gleason did the same thing later.

But this is what started our -- underneath, you know, because Leonard was not the kind of fellow to forgive and forget. The same thing with Woody Herman, but I never got any bad vibes from Woody. And in fact, they sent me a crate of oranges, which I ate, gladly. But never played Woody on the records.
In respect to me, there was no return address on those oranges, just said Woody Herman. So I just ate the oranges.
But I wasn't playing Woody Herman records. I didn't even -- this was another place where we fell out. I did not want to play the Lou Waters records.
Who wanted you to play the Lou --
Gleason and -- this was a revival thing coming on, and they brought them up, one or two, because --
You also said that they -- when you first started, they insisted that you read the script that they --
Exactly.
What they had programmed.

Read the script and play the records that we give you, and don't deviate. And I was improvising. Well, if I played an Armstrong record, I don't have to read everything they say about him. I lived with him, practically, for two years. So I'm going to say things personal.
But, anyway, this was becoming a source of irritation to them. And so in time, maybe three months or so, I lost them. Friendly, but we part.
And you kept the show.

And I kept the show. And I started collecting. Now I've become a record collector, and I never knew about it. I never knew about buying three records, if you were able to find them, even though you only need one, and trade the other two, for what you really need. I didn't know about that.
Well, I got hip very fast because I didn't have all

that many. I mean, I'm still making my living playing. But it was during that time that Dale Carr, who has written two books, Piano in the Band, and DUPREE Blues, was a printer by trade and author and an editor by inclination, approached me -- and a great piano fan, approached me about putting out a magazine.
Dale Curran, C-u-r-r-a-n.

Yeah, but I think you pronounce it Curran. Right, C-u-r-r-a-n. He's still around, retired somewhere, I hear, in Naples, Florida. But he approached me, he said he would do the work. All I had to do was get the musicians to talk, and we would put out a magazine like there isn't, in which the musicians talk and tell their story, word for word.

Well, that interested me. And we'd tell the people where they play, and not worry them about the records. Let that be -- Discography, let that to those magazines that do it so good. We'll just feature stories by and about. And we did get record reviews by George Avakian. He immediately volunteered. We got some great photo covers by -- I can't think of the name of them. One is the son of a great artist, American artist, and he's a great artist in his own right, great photographer in his own right now.
Well, I think of it because I've got the --
Peterson?

No, I think he might have contributed. But that was not the name. But in any case, we got beautiful pictures, we got stories, priceless stories. Cow Cow Davenport's story to me is priceless. He never wrote another thing in his life.
He actually wrote it?
Told it to us like I'm telling you. It was word for word.
And then did Curran --
Typed as fast as he wrote. We had no other way of doing it.
And he edited --
If there was any words. But with Cow Cow don't think there was any words. It was very simple. He didn't use --
And, of course, this magazine is The Jazz Record.
Jazz Record, which now became the book, Selections From the Gutter. But this was it. And we kept that going for 60 issues, over four years.
And when did you start it, '42?
We started in -- I think the first one was February, '43. And it lasted through November, '47.
Whose idea was it for the title, Jazz Record?

Probably not mine, because I'm not sure I would think of that. It was more like a newspaperman that would think of that than a musician. But Dale did most of the work for four years, until he finally gave it up. I'm talking about addressing envelopes, about bringing it to the printer, about reading type. The job I did was wonderful. I walked around like an editor, and I interviewed guys. I got them down in that basement, and we miraculously were always able to come up with a jug which now I think Dale always paid for. And whistle, and mine too, wet these guys and get them to talk.

And they would relax in front of me, because it's easy to relax in front of somebody in your own trade. It's easy for me to relax now, because I'm talking in front of someone who's a musician. And so that was the policy. And it worked out very well. And it didn't harm me. We got so popular, between the -- not that the magazine was selling so great, because of the radio. Because pretty soon I lost that radio show, anyway.
What - why did you lose it? (synagogue La Guardia)

I lost it because La had heard me again. The second time he heard it, there was nothing for me to do. He always went on the air before me. I followed all the symphony music, all the fire alarms that he chased and all that. He was a great one for chasing fires in New York. And all the things that he would have to tell New York, -- WNYC

was New York's own station. And everything he would have to do would be before me at 1:30. But on occasion, there would be some reason for him to -- and so the radio would be on in the room where he was. And the second time this was on, there was no explaining that I wasn't commercial and (inaudible).

And so, there went the program and there was no -- I couldn't change. I wasn't going to sit down and answer 30 letters or more a day. The kids were just -- I kept a lot of them, they were just writing and what was I -- this is that record that you called their number out and I want to get it and I missed it. Or, I enjoyed your program. They called for an answer, and I just wasn't going to do it.
So I just -- I blew it.
You would give it out on the air.
Yes, I would give it out on the air, which is the way it should be done.
Sure.

But he objected. So I lost the job. But in that time, I gained an audience, and I started running jam sessions in the Village. And we found a place that was just perfect for us. Seats that would slant up. And -- yes, theater type of thing, but it was actually a loft. And the -- a dollar apiece to get in. $20 for the leader, me, $10 for the men, by anybody who wanted.
My gosh, I don't know who I didn't have.
HEMLOCK
When was this?

This was '43, '44. Okay, Mezz, Pee Wee Russell, Rod Cless, I had all three. Trumpets, Max Kaminsky, Muggsy Spanier, Fred Allen, drums, George Wettling, or Freddy Moore or Kaiser Marshall, whoever was available. And Pops Foster always on bass.

Trombone, Sandy Williams, -- I don't know who else was around. But these were the musicians that -- Sidney Bechet, I had Sidney many times. In fact, I've got a story about Sidney. This was the first time I had Sidney. I hired him, I told him the date. Everybody showed up but Sidney. Well, I'm in a quandary. Here I advertised Sidney, and no Sidney. So I had my gopher who was helping me run around, and he comes back with two clarinet players, Mezz and Rod, to make up for it. So the people are happy.

Next week, I hire -- I don't know who. And that's the week Sidney shows up. Now I got two guys, and my temperament then was much different than now. I think -- I don't know whether I've improved in somebody's eyes. I haven't, they wished I'd of stayed that way. But, anyway, the way I was then, as far as I was concerned, Sidney could play all night and he wasn't going to get paid. Over my dead body, you go ahead.
And Sidney was mad, he was furious. And I had George Brunies, I remember. And George went to Harlem with

Sidney to keep him from coming back with his knife, because he said he was going to go home and get his knife. So -- but instead of which he took me to the union. And the union told me, and said we have been waiting to get this son-of-a-bitch for a long time. What is the story? And I told him.

He says, fine, you come up to the board with Sidney, we got a date. And when I found that out, I called Sidney and I says, I'm going to give you money. I don't want no part of that. For a lousy whatever-it-was, ten dollars, we're going to go in front of the union? It wasn't worth it. It was the best thing I ever did in my life, because when Blue Note decided to record with Sidney, and he was the man, then, although I was staff, he was the man. All Sidney had to say was 'no' -- and I was up. He said he had a good feeling towards me, and so we were very tight.
I think some of your best records are those that you're on, "Profoundly Blue" and the "Blue Horizon."
Yeah, he was tremendous. And he worked with me.
You said you were on a staff, at Blue Note?

Well, by that, I mean once they discovered that they could have me, and that they wanted me, then they started -- I was the staff pianist, so to speak. That didn't mean they owed me so much work. Every time they had a

date I was on piano, for the most part, if it was that kind of date. If it was what we called traditional jazz, I was on it. There was Edmond Hall on clarinet, where there was Albert Nicholas with Sidney Bechet or whether it was Sidney Bechet, or whether it was the Chicagoans, with Rod Cless, whatever it was. Or a New Orleans -- I can't name all the clarinet players.
(inaudible)
I recorded with more clarinet players than anybody else.
How did you get in with --

Alfred Lion? Well, Alfred Lion again was part of the aficionado scene. Alfred Ljon and Frank Wolff. They were both also in that Village scene, as was in part the Turkish ambassador's Ertegun sons, You could see their faces now and then.
Nesuhi and Ahmet Grmet.
But they were interested, very interested. And it was like a bunch.
Was Rudi Blesh around then, too?

Yes, he had come later. He'd gotten there in the '40s, the mid-'40s or close to the mid-'40s, he'd come to New York. And he'd started a show called This Is Jazz. So it was a jazz boiling pot at that time, and the only kind of jazz there was talk about was trad jazz, traditional jazz. And although it wasn't Dixieland as we see it, because trad

jazz included Lips Page on trumpet many times, and it included Harlem piano, so it was -- we were using the word with a fairly wide net. It wasn't a narrow -- and there were jazz aficionados that would call us a little bit beyond what it should be.
The purists.
Yeah, there were purists then, and I managed to stay -- although they bugged me, I managed to stay clear of them. But I did not understand the Lou Waters band at all, and it was hard for me to grasp.
That was the first imitating band, to imitate the King Oliver band. It was stupid, I think. And it's still going on.
Yeah, the imitators --
The real hard core jazz band. Kenny says they should carry surface noise with them.
Yes. So things were -- New York was the place, things was happening, there was no argument about jazz. We all knew what it was, it was the music that you struggled to make a living doing.

The first one was Edmond Hall. I remember that. It was probably High Society and it was a mixed date. Maxie might have been the trumpet player, -- Kominsky, and Edmond Hall, and --
Sidney deParis.

Sidney deParis, something like -- yeah, it might have been Sidney deParis. It was a driving band. That was the first date, I think. But then they started coming. They became very popular, in a very short time. And those records became popular. When they made the one with Wild Bill and Sidney Bechet, everybody thought, man, this is the greatest. This is what hot is, a hot band. And we were very --
Had that band ever worked together?
Never.
Just the records.

Just rehearsed and made the date. So into this scene the collectors, especially the Jazz Information, because I like to think of Ralph Gleason and Gene Williams and Rudy Blesh and people like that, began to reach out to do more. And they got him a trumpet. And they handpicked the band for him. And I think he had something to say about it, but --
George Lewis.
George Lewis, Jim Robinson and Baby Dodds.

And really appreciated what they did as a band. New York at that time, you could hear various sounds. You could walk down 52nd Street and see Barney Bigard playing with a small group at the Onyx. Well, again, that's what we were talking about earlier, you know, about brotherhood of jazz musicians, that doesn't exist --
Right, there's no quarrel.
(Recording interrupted.)

They seemed to -- Leonard particularly seemed to vent his spleen on you, as sort of symbolic of everything that they called the moldy figs.
Yes. Well, I had the Jazz Record magazine.
You were getting a lot of exposure.
A lot of exposure. Many Village people -- I had many so-called fans and people that really dug me and liked me, personally and musically.

So he made me a focal point, but not only me alone. Somewhere -- I read somewhere where he talked about Louis Armstrong's music being -- should have gone out with button shoes and Pee Wee Russell caught it from him. And this is one of the things that happened. Some of the musicians either didn't want to see what was happening, or wouldn't look at what's happening, as long as it wasn't happening to them.
Oh, some of the traditional --
Some of the traditional musicians. And not -- but Muggsy Spanier was not one of them. He read it loud and clear.
He punched Leonard out like that.
This is the story. Leonard came into Nick's, and Muggsy was playing there. And during intermission,

Muggsy walked up to him and started to tell him what he thought about him. And Feather reached in his pocket and pulled out some manuscripts. "But Muggsy, I came here to write and I love you and all." With that, he hit him, and Leonard ran. And he ran and Muggsy chased him. And ran around the block and saw a restaurant, a Greek restaurant, and ran in there and shut the door.

Well, the Greek -- you're not shutting my door during business hours. So somehow he saved Leonard's rear end and Muggsy let it go at that one punch. But the story is now going around the Village, amongst those guys, that that's what happened. But he wasn't the only one. Coleman Hawkins, I understand, grabbed him. Danny Alvin grabbed him. A bass player that went to jail because of pot, who played for this pianist whose father also played piano years ago.
Eddie Heywood?
Eddie Heywood. And I can't think of this bass player's name. He had a --
[John]
Simmons.
Simmons. They didn't draw the line.

There was no color line on who hit Leonard at that time. But the big story that I tell in this is the one about this friend of mine, -- oh, he wrote something in Jazz Record about Jimmy Noone's -- about Rodless going there or something like that, I can't think of his name. But he was a writer, he wrote for

political magazines, I think, or labor union magazines. He was in that kind of movement. But he loved that kind of jazz. He was a kind of drinking cat, liked to hang around with Rod Cless and Pee Wee and myself. And this was bothering him.

And one day, he was in the Village, and Bob Thiele, he runs into Bob Thiele, it was a Sunday. And Bob says to him, hey, do you know where I can get a job? It's Sunday. He says, no, what do you need a job for? The saloons aren't open. He says, well, there's this party going on, Leonard Feather and the Count whatever his name, from Sweden or Norway or something, -- I think they called him --
Oh, Baron --

Baron, yeah. Timmy Rosencrantz and the little guy from Vietnam or whatever his -- Harry Lim, and this whole crowd was gathered and George Simon's apartment. This, by the way, I have a feeling, is why I never got the Jazz Record published through the firm that George Simon is connected with, because I did show him the manuscript and I got a no.

But it was George Simon's apartment, and he wasn't there, Leonard was there. And that's a feeling I have. It may not have any veracity. But he let Leonard have the apartment. So my friend says, well, if you're going up there, I'd like to join you. He says, you won't like this crowd, it ain't your kind of -- forget it. I'll get the bottle and we'll

go up there.

So he got the bottle and they went up there. I mean, a fifth or whatever it was, a quart. And they were drinking, and he sat back in the rocking chair, and he heard all this chatter about this new world coming, new music and down with the old and all that. And he was getting irritated and didn't know what to do. And finally, he thought, well, he ought to break something, he ought to do something. And this big lamp standing next to the rocking chair. And he just rocked enough to knock over the lamp.

And Feather got up, just went and lost his mind. Oh, the lamp, I'll have to pay for it. And George Simon -- and my friend says to him, now, why are we making this big fuss? We can talk this over like gentlemen? Why don't you just come outside of all these people? Come outside. And there was about five or six steps down this building. And he came outside with him. And he says, now, what's all this about? He says, well, wait a second, are you really Leonard Feather? Of course, there's no other -- bam, he hit him and knocked him right down all the stairs. And hit him some more and then he started screaming. And Timmy came out and all those guys came out and my friend turned to him and he says, well, has he got any friends here? I would like a piece of the action.

So nobody wanted a piece of the action, and this fellow went away. This was all caused by all this writing that
Feather was --
It was a very bitter --
It was a bitter scene.
I think on both sides.
Both sides. It got out of hand.
Who started it?
Oh, the writer started it. Although Ralph --
The modernists?
It wasn't -- it was the writer. Feather was the first one that wrote anything. Now, why he started it is something else. Or whether he had cause.
It always seemed to me that there was a publicity motive behind it. If we could beat this --

It might very well, he was smart enough, Feather. He wasn't a dumb guy. Although Gleason said, when they asked him about it, he said, well, Jelly Roll must have kicked him in the ass sometimes, as an explanation.
Well, you eventually sued Leonard.

Well, let me finish this. Leonard sued this fellow who had beat him, and took him to court. Now, this fellow was very astute. After all, he was a labor man and he knew his way around. So he kept having the case postponed and -- until he got a good Irish judge. And this fellow was Irish. He got a good Irish judge and when the case came up before this
Irish judge, he told the judge that Leonard had accosted him. And the judge looked at Leonard, case dismissed, just cause.
I know Leonard has suffered those innuendos that he was homosexual, but I don't think he was.
I never thought one way or another. But this is how that case ended. Now, I sued him, sued him for $100,000. And --
When and why?

During that same period when I was getting smacked. Instead of taking to my fists, which I can't use very well, anyway, I found that out the hard way. I took him to -- I had a friend, a lawyer, who again I befriended the lawyer's son. And he says, sure, I'll take care of it. He told me I got a bad case; it's hard to beat him, but I'll try anyway.
Well, what did he say, now, defamation of character?
Yeah, yeah. And what happened was, Leonard settled out of court for $250 and court costs. And one subscription to Jazz Record. I insisted on it. That's all I wanted out of him.

I remember reading something -- I think it was Leonard who wrote it. I think it was in Metronome. Either accusing you or by implication accusing you of being Communist because you played for a labor union that was Communist-dominated -- a guild, newspaper guild or something like that.
Well, Ralph Toledano wrote a -- some few things for us, and we knew that he was to the right of the

right, but he also attracted people who were to the left of the left, to write for us. I never asked them what their politics was. My record was very clear that I was from the wrong side of the tracks, according to wealth, I was a working man. That's where my feelings lie, and so I was going to vote Democrat every time I could. I never voted Socialist, but I figured the Demmies were the best of two evils and they were better for the working class. They could look that record up. In fact, our phone was tapped for a long time.
Your phone was tapped?

The Jazz Record phone was tapped, because -- well, the government, no doubt because of the people -- at that time, the Village was a hotbed of kids that were becoming radically -- who were radically-inclined Russian lovers, because after all, --
We were in the war.
We were in the war. We were buddy-buddy.
Bundles for Russia.

Right. And I was getting jobs from these funny-named organizations. The Youth for America. I don't care, I don't want to -- they're giving me a job for a mixed band, and I need the work. I don't care what the morals are. I accept the work.
I finally broke with these people in a way. They gave me a job in a place called Camp Unity, and I'm writing

about that. In Camp Unity, it was outside of New York. And it paid very well for those times, and I could have a mixed band. I had Sandy Williams, Kaiser Marshall, Cecil Scott, Herb Ward, Henry Goodwin and myself.
At that time, just for a little clarification, was it still difficult to book a mixed band in New York?
Very. To me, it was very -- not difficult, it was difficult to book any kind of a band. But me wanting a mixed band --
Made it worse.

-- make it worse. For example, I had a job at the Astor Hotel. Ten men. I decided to find the ten best musicians I could find who were out of work on a Saturday. So it turned out, seven was black, three were white. Mezzrow, Jack Bland and Art Hodes. I couldn't get Rod Cless.
Yeah, and there's some question about Mezz.

Yeah. But, you see, if you go to get the best, you find that the best is out of your reach, because they're making more money that you can afford to pay them. So you get the best that are black, even though it's going to be hard on you. Because if you don't get the best, I'm talking about that time when, if you went on a train with blacks, you had problems, and I was doing it. I was travelling with them
and I had all sorts of problems.
That was true in the South but that was true in New York, too.

Yeah. And on top of that, I loved to play with those guys. I was doing it for many reasons. Okay, I've got this job at Camp Unity. And I'm only there about ten minutes, so to speak, when I know that this is a Commie camp. It's obvious. They run up the American flag, but and we're not at war with Russia, we're at peace. I think this is '47, something like that, and they're passing out literature and attracting all these young gals, like, one young gal says, I couldn't dance with a Negro in New York, but here I can do it.

So it wasn't only dance. It was the free love or whatever it was. It was the freedom that they had in the world that were attracting a lot of working class people. Now, me, I wasn't interested. They gave me a job. What got me interested was when they started stepping on my toes. They started following me around. I'm not going to name the people, at least, one who I knew, that went to Hollywood and made it big in music, different people that were in that camp. And they had no trouble like I did. They were members, I wasn't a member.

But they followed me in the bathroom, stand on either side of me on the urinal. Why don't you join the Party? I said, I can't afford to, I need the capitalistic press. And

they says, are you kidding? So the next day, I'm at the toilet, the same two guys and they can show me in papers where this guy belongs, this guy belongs, and he also needs the capita-listic press. I can't do it.

And they were getting hot at me. And I was no easy target. They caught us in the band room, and the fellows were playing dice. They went into hysterics: You can't do this here, this is not intellectual. If you want to play chess -- I says, this is our castle. Whatever room we have as a band room is our castle. Don't come in and tell us what to do. And then they start getting me about, why don't you attend an economics class? I said, I will if you show me how we can get more money from you guys for the band.

So they were mad with me, and they ran me out. What they did was, they had a meeting, almost like I was in Russia and I was pulled before the board. And they said, he's got to go. And so I left the band, they replaced me, and I went back to New York. They weren't through with me, now that they were hot at me. So they offered me a job, again, another title, Young Women of America.

Obnoxious, I don't know who they are, but they give me a deposit, a union contract. They hire me and I got Max Kqminsky and I got Chippy Hill, I got -- and I go to the newspapers and I get a plug in the columns. In a week, I see an ad in the paper: The Young Women of America who so success-
fully produced the Paul Robeson concert in New Jersey. That was a riot in New Jersey, that concert. It was a big riot and a lot of problems.
It came out that Robeson was a Communist.

Was a Communist. And it really caused a stink. So I went to the same writers of the newspapers, and I told them what had happened. And I says, as far as I'm concerned, there's the contract, and I tore it up, I will not be there. And that's how I broke with them. They stopped giving me jobs. But they were really on my tail.
You said that the telephone in the Jazz Record was --
That was tapped.
By whom? FBI?
We never found out. What we could tell --
How did you know that?

Well, we knew that -- you could pick up the phone, there was always a click where it had never been before. And I don't know, it's -- somebody just figured that the wrong people were coming in to see Jazz Record, the people -- the folk singers, Pete Seeger or all those people, because they were in the Village, too. And they knew who -- my agent called me in one time and said, Art, we got a little trouble
* Paul Robeson was never a member of the Communist Party, as is popularly believed. He did, however, perform in Party and leftist sponsored programs.

here. The government would like to know -- through me, I've been asked if you know -- and I told Freddy, I says, Freddy, I'm clean as a whistle. I don't know anybody. I don't vote Communist, they can look at my record. I don't vote Socialist. I vote Democratic, been doing it for years. And I says, I'm not in that bag.

And, sure, I've watched those guys, I've heard their talk. I don't get away from them, just like when they talked too ethereal, French paintings or something. What do I know about that? I walk away. They make me uncomfortable. I'm a musician, I'm into music, and if I just handle this one thing, fine. That doesn't mean I'm dumb to what's going on in this world politically, and that I don't have some thoughts about it.

But I ain't going to join any Party like that. That ridiculous. Especially now, I've been to East Germany, I saw what that -- I saw the Wall. That makes me sick to see that. They're not offering us a better solution to living. I'm a believer that you've got to get in and clean it up. In other words, I'm not against the union. I think our union needs help. But I think I should get in and help it from the inside, not go to the newspapers and scream about our stinking union. That ain't the way to do it.
