And it's the same way with government. You don't like it, see what you can do with it. But this is a hell of a

country, and that's the way I felt then and that's the way I feel now. But on the other hand, I don't go as far to the right as George Brunis did which, he read the Chicago American, and that was the extent of his political beliefs. I'm not that naive, for me, to think that way. There's a lot of things wrong.

Kenny was talking about Brunis the other night, saying that he and his Dick Welstood were having what he described as a very delicate conversation wherein the Cuban crisis -- and everybody in New York, those missiles were going to be sent out. And he said, Brunis just barged in and heard what they were talking about and said, drop a bomb on and that'll stop all that shit.

It was common talk. I'm not saying anything about George that hasn't been talked by all musicians. Everybody who knew George knew that the extent of his reading matter, probably, was the Chicago American, it was easy to read, they had some good jokes there, a puzzle and things like that. And plus, he didn't have a great deal of education and that was it.

But I knew the country was in bad shape, the country's in bad shape now. I mean, the world is in bad shape. The world's in bad shape. It's obvious. But joining the Communist Party is not going to cure it.
Yeah, but apparently part of the
arsenal that the -- Leonard and the others used to get you, it was a personal attack, almost.

Yeah, it had no veracity. If they'd said that I like girls, he had something. If he said that I smoked pot, he had something. I smoked a lot of pot, I loved it. If he said I drank, fine, when I could get ahold of it, yes. This, he had something. This is true.
But to say -- why didn't he say that I jammed with Pres, Lester Young? Why didn't he say that?
You said that he cost you a record date.

That cost me a record date. Well, Harlem recording outfit, where there was -- I can't remember the title, got very interested in doing blues with Lester Young and Art Hodes. Only they told me over the phone, don't do no sadass blues. Do blues that are -- got some brightness and yet feeling, but let it jump a little.

So that we could sell. We had it set up. I had no paper, but I had his word and I had all these conversations. And when he read that article, he called me up the next day and says, I'm sorry, I can't go through it.
What article was that? -in Down Beat-
Leonard wrote in Metronome that he could play me under the table, that I was -- oh, it was a terrible writeup. We have it, by the way. We have a copy of it, and

it'll go in the book. To show-- and I probably won't write the chapter, I'll just write the chapter I related about this incident that happened between my friend and things like that. But Chet, who is an educator and an English prof at the Circle [University of Chicago] campus will look up all the material which he now has and put it down as a --
Does he have the diary that you kept during this time?
I've got it.
You've still got it.
I've still got a diary. And I can't find all the screaming words, but I found one piece of paper where I says, what is he, God? I have decreed what jazz is and what isn't.

Well, you know, anybody put themselves in your place, I know I could, that if I was playing, a musician playing, and there was this one writer that every time I played was going to write something derogatory about me, my God --

But you don't know the worst part about it. Let me tell you the worst part, which will go in the book. Is, I got a writeup in Look magazine, and I still have that, in which he reviewed Selections From the Gutter. And it was a very complimentary thing.
The book or the record?

The record. He says, a sincere piano solo by Art Hodes, Russian-born Art Hodes. Blues flavor and all that. There wasn't a bad thing there. He doesn't say I'm a great pianistic pianist. But there's nothing bad about the rendition.

I think -- it's my opinion that Milt Gabler, who was putting it out on Commodore, got Leonard to do this, and they inserted it. There was ten records reviewed. Mine was the bottom one, by Look. And I don't know if this is true, but I think that it was Milt that got him to do this. This was pre-argument, before this thing.

Another unfortunate thing, I think, came out of that. And I felt that even in Louisville, Kentucky, because musicians were reading this all over the country. The schism that grew between the guys that wanted to play bebop and the guys that wanted to play traditional or whatever.
That's right.
What was the relationship in New York between, say, yourself and Charlie Parker and Dizzy?

Well, I didn't know Charlie. And Dizzy came just after -- Dizzy and Charlie came in about 1947, and I didn't have anything to do with it then, didn't know them. But the other musicians that were getting plaudits, you didn't see them playing with us as much or anymore.
You mean, plaudits from --

From the press people, yeah. Because your heart is where your money is, and they're making their living there. And so there seems to be a separation now. There's a coolness that's coming. But more than that, think of the tragedy of the great clarinetists, Jimmy Noone, who never made number one on the poll.

They become thrown in the ashcan. That's the whole style. And ten years of their lives is taken away from them, because if you don't work, if you -- did you ever read the liner notes that Studs Terkel wrote for Columbia Artists on Big Bill Broonzy's appearance in Niagara or some town? Studs loaned it to me. He's booed by his own people, he's booed out, because of the music. He's old-fashioned, he's old hat.

I worked the Capital Lounge in Chicago, and I got what we call a Dixieland setup, clarinet, trombone and trumpet. But I got Buddy Smith on drums. Buddy has played with Diz, he's played with the Bird, he's played with Zut and now he's playing with me. He's a good drummer.

So the audience is black. We hit a two-beat number, and the audience clears out and is in the street. And then Buddy and I do a number together, and they come back. And let me tell you another instance. I'm booked in a place called Stars of Jazz, New Stars of Jazz, in Chicago, right near the Union Station. The Rising Stars of Jazz, that's what it was.
And Lena -- what was this girl singer that come out
Carmen McRae?
No, no, smaller name. But, no -- anyway, she has a club of her own on the South Side now.
Oh, Lurleen Hunter.
Lurleen Hunter is playing there. Les Strand is playing piano and Parker or something like that, a big black pianist; I don't know. Anyway, he's still around playing cocktails.
Les Strand, by the way, is back in Chicago.

So there are -- this is the club and I'm booked there, playing off nights, for both the organist and the piano. I go into a two-beat number, 'Ballin' the Jack' or something, and the house started shuffling their feet, getting up, moving around. I play 'Washboard Blues' and there ain't a sound. I play any ballad and they sit there now beautiful that thing was. They don't move.
(Laughter)

But the minute I play two-beat, out they go. And this was what has happened because of this. That's bad, but the real bad part was, like, Big Bill Broonzy and putting him out of work, and putting all these great players, take ten years out of the life. This is what I objected to, in retrospect.
Yeah. But don't you think that's

The whole scene is changing, because the youth today doesn't want to know nothing about it. They want to pick up a kazoo, don't tell me nothing about it, how you play the kazoo, or a banjo, anything. The new age -- they're not into it.

In fact, Feather now is getting put down. I read something where somebody called him moldy. Because naturally, how can you keep on going? There's somebody that you came in on the scene with, and that to you identifies you. Those are your people. Meanwhile, the world moves on. Twenty years later new people come on the scene and they've got nothing to do with you. It's like, this says, do you know that Miles Davis now has to tell people who I am?
Well, it's ridiculous in art. And in other art forums it's not as bad as it is or was in jazz. You must destroy the old and go on to -- whatever is new is better.

But you said something before that these people who did it were not true people to their own beliefs. In fact, they were taking money for plugging people that they were supposed to be criticizing or writing critical analysis on.
That was just Leonard at the time. He was working as a press agent for Duke Ellington, and at the same time, he was reviewing Ellington concerts and writing about
Ellington in Metronome.
Right.
And as a professional, I find that appalling.
And didn't you also say that, Gleason later on did it on the West Coast?
Yeah. Duke Ellington and Ray Charles. And when I found out about it, and I was at DownBeat by then, I would not let him write about those people. Because I found out that he was on their payroll.
Well, this is what --
It was unethical. Stanley Dance the same way.
This is what I thought, that there was no -- if you want to criticize -- well, this is the trouble with this. Because of Leonard, then you get a Stanley Dance coming along a little later in his camp.
Oh, I don't think Stanley is in Leonard's camp.
No, but I got a review of a record with Barney Bigard , and he just was almost crying when Barney made that record with me.
Should have been with an Ellington group or something.
Yes, yeah, he was almost crying. But I see so much throwbacks to the old.

There's still some of the old-fashioned critics, if you want to call them that, and I know them all and I consider them my friends. But it's still -- I was saying old-fashioned. But to me, it is unethical for Stanley for all those years to be on Ellington's payroll and writing about Ellington, interviewing the sidemen as he did for me in DownBeat, is one thing. But to review an Ellington record as he did in the Saturday Review, or write about a performance in nothing but glowing terms -- and now the same thing is true with Stanley and Earl Hines. He works for Earl Hines.
Sure.

So I can't believe anything that Stanley writes about Earl Hines or, when Duke was alive, about Duke. Now, he's a great officiator and he doesn't see it as a conflict of interests. He sees it as -- he loves those people, he loves the music. But to me, he's still is unethical. And I love Stanley.
Yeah. If you was in government and they found that out they'd get rid of you because you've got a conflict of interest.

But, anyway, what I'm trying to say is, and hope to say, saying is that this is what we had to grow through, growing pains, whatever it was, and some of us survived it. But there was quite a few players that couldn't rise to this, and took to driving a cab or a day job or something. Drove them out of
the business, from --
Yeah, it was a very vicious, hurtful thing.

It was just too bad. We didn't have a Norman Granz to take us around in concerts. We had nobody. We had an Eddie Condon, who was doing what he could for the few in New York, and Ernie Anderson. This is what we had. And so that we survived this in itself, because the new age don't want nothing about that. And I'm not -- I think this should be stated historically, this is what happened. But I have no bones to pick, if I could do it without mentioning Leonard's name, that would be well with me, too. I'm thinking, it's just the historical thing to happen, we should know about it. There was a jazz war. It wiped out a lot of traditional jazz players, as far as continuing in the business as a playing performer. Just wiped them out, made part time musicians out of them, or completely out of it. And when I think of the horror, I think it's terrible. And I think especially of people like Jimmy Noone, never having amounted to what he should have amounted to. He should have been so much. To me, he was as important as Tatum was to the piano, to that New Orleans style clarinet.
Yeah, but he unfortunately died just as that rivalry was getting going.
Yeah, but they didn't glorify him while
it was -- there was no glory for him in the '40s.
That's true.

Well, I just name one. Don't you think it hurt Edmund Hall? Sure, Louis gave him some work and all that, but don't you think it hurts -- okay, take me. I look on the polls and I don't see my name on there, time after time after time. It never appears. And for the longest time, I wasn't even in the Who's Who in Jazz that was put out.
Who's Who? Well, Teo was putting it out.

It's only later that they figured the hatchet had been buried deep enough in my head, let it go and go ahead. But even when I was in California and sat across from him, and then when we left town the writeup followed us again. It was Jim Beebe that showed me the writeup, told me about it. That he was still after me. He says, you should read the writeup. He says, the band was the Chicagoans, and the only guy there that played anything good was the guy that wasn't from Chicago, Barney Bigard.

And he still had that little poke at the music. And so I didn't get back to Disneyland. I talked to that man, we were very close friends. And there was a good feeling between the man that booked us and me. But after that, I never reached him. I thought maybe he'd lost the job or something. This is what the press can do. They can hurt you very badly. You're

part of the press, you know that the power of the press -- for example, I have a friend who just died, Veria? Wilson. And he would talk about a certain musician, I won't name him, who was a bandleader, who has a son who takes care of the books. And every time he gets paid, there's money missing off his payroll.
And he says, I'd rather beat him with a sword in his hand than a pen.
(Laughter.)

And to me, that shows how mighty than pen is. You sit down and -- you could retract all you want. For example, this last DownBeat, the review of my book, Selections From the Gutter, that was totally -- the wrong guy reviewed it. It's not that it should be glorified, but at least it should be reviewed by somebody that doesn't hate that period in history or doesn't put it down, doesn't want to know anything about it. It should be somebody that could be fair about it, could remove himself and review it.
So the pen to me has always been mighty, and this puts the musician in a very dire spot, because he can't put the pen down because he might need him.
Well, you're one of the few musicians who write, and write very well. How did you get into that?
By force. Curran got me involved. He says, all you have to do is sit down and if it needs help,

I'll help you. Write something about your life. Just like you're playing, talk. Just like you're talking, write. So he -- every move I've made that has advanced me is somebody jabbing me in the ass to go forward. It's like a very religious -- I don't think that's a good word, a spiritual priest I met once, I says to him, how come that you have become so tuned in on this stuff? He says, it's from doing that, and he pointed down, like the devil, that I'm doing this. Somebody just poked me and poked me --
With a pitchfork.

With a pitchfork so I went in the other direction. Well, it's the same thing. I was poked to write. I didn't one day get up and say, I'm going to be a writer, a jazz writer. Robert Allen Arthur? says of the two musicians that are writing, I was one of the two, the other he says was Louis Armstrong that he cared to read. He wouldn't care to read any other. And he's a writer.

So I feel complimented by it. It doesn't turn my head too much, because I realize that I better stick to playing music. I'm not going to make it writing. But it's good. I think the musician who can be audible should be, should say it. But don't get involved, don't suddenly think you've become a writer. You're a writer of a subject that you know something about. And if you can stick to that, you'll do well. And to the extent that well can be done doing that, that's fine.
Don't get carried away.
There were several musicians that --
Rex Stewart comes to mind right away.

Rex was a good writer, all he had to do was take the first two pages of his manuscript and throw those away, and then after he got through with all the pretensions, because he could be quite pretentious in his writing, --
Oh, yeah.

-- and a little pompous. And I just take all that out. And then when he got talking about Bix or about Fletcher Henderson or Duke or whatever, that was good, that was great. And I had to get rid of all of the writer stuff.
I didn't know that.
Well, not many people do. In fact, --
I loved his writing, and I thought, my, where does he get that talent? Because so few guys were bright.
Well, he had talent. It was just that -- I don't know, a lot of people have the idea that if you're going to be a writer, you must be profound.
Oh, cripes.
And so he'd go through that. And every one I'd take out, the next one would come in, it'd be the same thing.
Well, he wrote very-- there's a few people
that -- one of the greatest things I've read by a musician was the one that Louis Armstrong did, not about Louis, but Louis Armstrong talking, and it came out, finally, in a very small booklet.
Yeah. There was supposed to be a series of them, and only this one came out.

It may have been something that he did for Life magazine, it might have been an interview or some thing. But it's a very small booklet. And where he talks about the early funerals, where the body was in the back room of somebody's place and he said, they didn't know too much about burials there, about preparing the body. And sometimes that body would jump a little. And he says, we'd clear out of there the whole place would run out the door.
I've found that musicians were better writers than the so-called jazz writers. And I don't mean that they wrote with more feeling or warmth. They just wrote better.
Now, Leonard Feather is a very good writer, in my estimation, a good craftsman.
Journalese.
What did you say, he's a good craftsman?
Good craftsman.
Yeah, from where I set, I read him and I have to say, well, man, he writes good. It's what he says
or doesn't say where I'm suspect. But his writing, I can't say that -- and the --
But you suspect his motives because of what you know of his history.
And the amount of work he's --
And I never know what connection he's got with the artist he's writing about.
And the amount of work he puts out.
Well, he's a very fast writer. He will sit down at the typewriter and it'll just comes out.

Who else put out a Who's Who on jazz? Year after year, and things like that. To a certain extent, a lot of that is important, because if he doesn't hate you, you might get a lot of factual stuff there. At least, I don't know who else is doing it.
Well, it's a good record.

That's what I mean. That I don't want to put him down. But I'd just as soon let him rest, except that we are putting out a book and the story of the jazz war will be in there. If I have to take the book to a country publisher.
Yeah, I've talked to Leonard about that period, and I've always had the impression that he'd rather not talk about it, that it really wasn't as bad as everybody makes it out, and -- I love Art Hodes.
Well, I'm very glad that he loves me.
That's the feeling that I get from him.

But I used to have an agent that loved me very much, but he never could get me any work. I says, well, with friends like that, who needs enemies? It's the same thing. But I understand this word love, you know. Nothing in the world I wouldn't do for you. The result is, he does nothing. I don't need that. So I'd rather he wouldn't love me. Just don't write about me, leave me alone, because I can't get no help in that way.

But I can see his point about wanting to forget that whole period. Naturally, if I was him I'd want to forget it. It's not going to throw a good light on him. He wasn't a very nice person. What he did wasn't very nice, to a lot of people, not only to me, but to a lot of people.
I understand that he changed, his personality changed, became more mellow, after he had a very serious accident in which he and Jane, his wife, were seriously injured.
That could be.
And people who have known him for years, like John Hammond told me that Leonard changed after that. He'd come very near death.
That could be.
And that philosophical --
Well, the light could have shined and said to him, Leonard, did you feel that pitchfork? It's time to change.
Well, let's go back to your --

Well, I'm back to New York. All this is a New York happening. There's an involvement, there's a life there, it's alive. Even getting into all this trouble was an alive thing. It did not run me out of the business, didn't run me out of town. I was still able to find some --
Do you think that it helped you some? In getting work from the so-called moldy fig side of things?

Well, they were in my corner, anyway, whatever work -- and I was a promoter. If I'd never made it in music, I probably would have gone in for promo. I like to see something happening from nothing. I'm very attracted to that.

So but I wasn't going to lay down and die. I'd find something to do. And there were still trad places tha were going to run trad music. Jimmy Ryan's was still going to run, the Vanguard still used trad music, in spite of it. And there was outlying places. So I was able to work. And Nick gave me a few jobs here and there, not steady, because he had his favorites. I just wasn't one of his favorites. The

same with Condon. I was about fifth on his list. But that's got nothing to do with it. He was fifth on my list of guitar players. This is a thing that a person should be allowed to have, his favorites. If I talk to you about your favorite clarinet player and if I was a clarinet player I might be sixth.
Just to go off on a tangent here, you mentioned earlier that Jess Stacy was always helping you to get jobs back in the old days in Chicago.
Right.
You mentioned clarinet players and piano players and so forth. And Jess, you said, tried to get you into Benny Goodman's band when he was leaving.
Yeah.
Tell me about that.

I followed Jess through numerous jobs. He's been very kind to me. And then one day I got a call that Benny Goodman was coming down to work, I was playing, I was playing with Rod Cless, someplace in Chicago, 5100 Club or something, 5100 North Broadway. And Baby Frank Snyder was playing drums.

Everybody got very excited, and I said, what's all the excitement about? Benny Goodman. So, who's Benny Goodman? He's got a big band. I wasn't interested. I was interested in small bands, even then. He came with John Hammond and he came with this girl singer and I think at that time it was Helen Forrest.

And everybody -- the King was here, the whole place they're running to his table. I didn't run to his table, because I remember him as a kid. See, we were kids at Hull House, and his bandmaster brought him in to where I was playing for the dancers. And he asked me if I minded if the kid played with me. And I looked at this kid, with a head that seemed so outsized and even though the head was outsized, the ego was outsized, too. And he had such an assurance, and just a tilt of the nose, almost.
About how old was he then?
Oh, if I was 12, he was nine. I don't know. How much difference, but I was just -- if I was a teenager, he had to be 13. Just very -- so whatever he was, in relationship to me. But he could play.

But I wasn't that impressed, because -- I says, yeah, you play nice. I didn't hear no great ideas. I've never heard anything out of him that I want to go down the street and whistle, as I have with Louis Armstrong. I have with Bix, I have with any number of people. I never heard a thing out of him that I -- I've even heard with Tatum, that little introduction or little something going on that I want to sing when I get out. I never heard that with Benny.
But I heard that he knew his instrument, but that didn't impress me that much. I wasn't impressed with that nonsense. And that's the time we met. So when I saw him
again, the only memory I had of him was this. And I was -- Rod Cless was my man and he was in the band. I was with Rod.

So they send this girl up to sing. Now, I don't know I'm being auditioned. Haven't the slightest idea, although Jess told me, he's coming to town. But I figured he's coming in to sit. Or if I'm auditioned, to call me to the table, sit down and talk. None of that. He hears the band play, and the girl goes up to sing with me, and I'm playing the blues. And I won't deviate.
(Recording interrupted.)

-- give her an opening. And I'm not about to give her an opening because I'm deep in what I'm doing, I'm playing the blues. You want to sing the blues, sing the blues. I'm not stopping you. She just sat at my feet for about five til I got through playing the blues then they minutes, ten minutes, went back to the table. After that, they called for their check and went out.

And that's all I -- I never heard another word. And I thought it was one of the greatest moments, looking back, in my life. I was so thankful, because I avoided that. I didn't need that. That isn't my bag. I want to play and enjoy myself playing. So maybe it kept me from going up the ladder because I didn't go through the ranks. And I thought of that. But there's a price you pay for everything. You want to enjoy what you're doing in music, then you're going to have to forego some of the other things.
Sure.

I got involved in a big band once, through Eddie Condon. It was Joe Marsala's big band, at Loew's Nose as he called it, Loew's State Theatre. And I've seen that big band. And I remember that saxophone section, after every show rehearsing. 29 shows, they rehearsed after every show, trying to get that break right.

It was a 32-bar tune, and at the end of the 29th bar, there was a two-bar break, and one of the saxophone players was supposed to come in. Now, if I may say, there was a beat like this, boop, and then he was supposed to come, boop-bee. He never made it. He never made it on time. And they're back there scuffling Joe Marsala finally made him the band boy after that. He felt sorry for him.

But this was my experience, hearing saxophones, and every note I hit has to correspond with what those seven saxophones are playing, and whether I'm not capable, or whether I just don't care to do it, it's not my bag. So I stayed out of it, and I was glad. It was no disappointment on my part. If it was the Benny Goodman Quartet, it would have been a disappointment. But it was not, it was taking Jess's place.

And the funny thing about Jess, he talked to me recently. Benny wanted him to go to New York for that concert. And he offered him $1800. And Jess says, well, now, let me see, I'm going to be there five days. New York hotels, I won't

travel without my wife, so I got to pay the airfare both ways. I don't have any winter clothes, and it's winter. So I'm going to have to go -- and themore he thought about it, the more the answer came out no. And he told him no, it's not enough money.

But I knew beyond that, it wasn't all the money. He just did not want that experience again. He just had had it. He was delighted with his life. And it was the same Jess that, when he picked up my book and read it, he wrote me a letter that I've still got, just glowing, knocked him out, to find that the story about him was there, just as he had said it.

The relationship with musicians, as you say, is a brotherhood, with no color, no -- and that remains, in spite of the critics. We have outlived that. They've done their worst and we're still together. I'm not sure that Leonard and Ulanov are buddy-buddy. I would be interested to find out.
I have a feeling that they're not. Barry went off into something -- he was quite intellectual, was teaching at a college in New York. I guess he still is, English literature.

But the musicians have gotten closer, if anything. Oh, there are certain ones that we don't want to be around, when you start talking, because -- let's get together. Well, I've got to tell you this story about critics, because you would appreciate it and it's part of the history.
Charles Edward Smith at that time in our period in New York was getting some acclaim as a writer.
He was writing for Esquire; as was Leonard.
Right, and the book that he wrote, or part of a book.
The Jazz Record Book.

And he was also taking a little weight on in his head, where he was getting a little heavy to be around. And after all, we all hung out at Julius' Bar and Grill, which was around the corner of Nick's. And that's where we got our mail, it was our country store, it was our library, this was it. Eddie Condon would wheel his baby up and leave her outside in the buggy and he'd go inside. And this is where we lived, part of the day.

And Charles Edward hung out there, which was getting to be a pain in the ass to Eddie. And Eddie's got a good mind, so he started thinking, what are you going to do about it? So he set this up. And Smith came in one night, and he introduced this guy, who looked like a Russian. Might have looked a little like Kenny Davern with a moustache, and a little hat. "This is Vladimir Steenevitz, a great Russian jazz critic. And this is Charles Edwards Smith, great American writer, jazz critic. Oh, glad to know you. And the Russian says to him, what do you play? And Smith says, I don't play nothing." And the Russian looks at him and says, in Russia, we
shoot you.
(Laughter.)
And that was it. From then on, we got along very well with Smith. He got the point after awhile, because we broke up, the whole bar broke up and they just -- it was just too much.
So when did you come back to Chicago? And what were the circumstances? What had been happening in Chicago from what we'd been talking about earlier?
Okay, now we go back to 1949. Pee Wee and Art have opened up Pee Wee and Art's Back Room. Phil Harris is coming in on a Friday night and fooling with the forks. He's a drummer.
Comedian (laughter)

Yes. And we're beginning to attract people. Eddie Condon gives us a show on television, Pee Wee and Art's Back Room, gives us George Wattley gives us, like, a quick two-number shot. Well, we're getting known, and the joint is beginning to fill up. We're getting a $30 a week draw, $35. Pee Wee never got too much because I stopped drinking then, and Pee Wee didn't. So Pee Wee's money always went for the booze, and my money was going to support the family. And we'd moved out of the town a little bit. We had some children. It's a good thing I stopped.
How many children --
At that time, we had three and one was on the way. We had six children, but five lived. I lost one, that was a tragedy, one of the tragedies we had. But -- 19 months old.

Anyway, so I was getting a little more money all the time. So I was getting a little more money all the time. I wound up getting $110 a week before I left. And during that time, like I say, we booked Jack Teagarden and his whole band, in which we had a new clarinet player every night, even if we had to send to Philadelphia for him. And we had Lips Paige came in every Friday religiously, if he wasn't working in Blue. Red Allen came in, for free.

And they all supported us. The drinks were very nominal. It wasn't a big deal, it was a very small room. 90 people in that room, you had to sit in one another's laps. And Pee Wee would sit at any table. I told Pee Wee, now, don't worry about it, don't even think about it. When I go up there with Herb, wherever you're sitting is good. But --
With Herb?
With Herb Ward, the bass player. But do carry your clarinet, so if you feel like blowing, start blowing from the table. It sounded good, looked good.
And that's what we did. And then we got Willie the Lion Smith, we grew in stature. We got Chippy Hill, we got Willie. It got to be a place to go.
And just about the end of December, Freddie Williamson again calls me.
He's in Chicago?
He's in Chicago, and now he's Glaser's man, second in command. Would you want to come to Chicago, to the Blue Note? With the Dixielanders? We want to do something here.

And you get the band, but don't tell me the plan. He just tells me to get the band. Offers me $225 for myself and $175 for the men. I haven't seen $225 since I've been in New York. Even in accumulation, I haven't seen it. I'm driving a car that my wife sold before I left New York for five dollars. A Ford, that same Ford.
The same one you --
The cops are stopping me and saying to me, you look sad behind the wheel. I have to curb it to stop it because --
When was this, now, 1950?

1949 is when we left. '50, I left. I have to curb it, I don't have brakes, I can't afford them. We're not -- just ain't doing it, man, I don't know. My father put up the money for the house or we wouldn't have had a house. Money was something I had no quarrel with, I just didn't have any.
So here $225 is offered me. And the front all-star
group. Fine, I'm going to take Pee Wee Russell, I got Freddie Moore, he'll come, I'll take Chippy Hill, how many more? That's enough, we'll pick the rest of them in Chicago.

Fine, get to Chicago, okay, give you -- you can have Floyd O'Brien, if you want him. Okay, I want Floyd. Trumpet, give you Lee Collins. Fine, we can't afford no bass, that's it. And we're playing, and it's tremendous. Because we're working opposite either Errol Garner, Sarah Vaughan, we're working opposite those kind of people so the joint is packed.
But this was the first Blue Note.
First Blue Note.
And where was that located?

This was on -- I don't know if it was the first or the second. It was on Madison Street, and I think it was down in the basement. That was it. And they played Louis Armstrong in that place. Now, the plan starts to unfold here, I didn't know when I got when I hired these guys. And the plan is that we're going to replace Freddie Moore with Zutty Singleton. We're going to replace Lee Collins with Wild Bill Davis. We're going to replace Floyd O'Brien with George Brunis. And we're going to get Bechet to get on and get offstage, as a star.
Holsteins
Whose plan was this, Frank Holsteins?
No, Freddy Williamson, because Louis
Armstrong has got his band, the small band on the road, and it's a big deal. Let's build the Dixielanders, and if they want Louis, they got to take the Dixielanders next. That's the clout.
The old ABC booking....
Yeah. And the next time around, you don't have to worry, we'll kill them. They'll take us, anyway. That's the -- now I got to tell Freddie Moore he's through.
That's what eventually killed the Blue Note, according to Frank Holstein. If you wanted Duke, you had to take Joe Blow.

What it did to me was, I got zutty. Now, last time I worked with zutty was on Decca Records. And zutty and I were very together. But now, here I'm not drinking, I'm not smoking, I'm not -- very straight kick. And probably not playing as good, because it takes a while to start -- if you've been playing high and drunk all the time, you get sober, not drink and not get high, it's going to take you a while to find your way around. And that I have to admit, I can't fault nobody.

The other end of the stick is, zutty is way out. I'm not talking about him smoking pot. I mean, he's out there, he's doing something. If it's that much off, a hairline off, it bothers him. Just -- or the tempo or the way I'm playing. And we were not together, right from the start.
Now, I got in off the plane, I took him to my

brother in law's house, I saw that he ate, I took him with his drums to the Blue Note, I set him up. I was a Zottie fan. And within days, he's not talking to me. And he's mad at me, which is worse, and he's evil.

Now that's going on. Now they start to drinking. I've got George Brunis, one Saturday night, five bottles are consumed, either three pints or three fifths, or two pints -- whatever it is, between who? Pee Wee, Zotty, George Brunis, maybe Chippy had a sip or something. She wasn't great on drinking. So this was going on. And Frank Holstein -- now, George Brunis is getting up in front of the mike, and Frank says to me, whatever you do, I don't care what else you do, beat him to the mike. To try to beat George Brunis, and Sarah Vaughan is waiting to go on.
And George grabs the mike away from him. And says, 'my mother thinks I'm selling stolen cars in Pittsburgh, but I'm not as you can see. I want to tell you about a tune I wrote.'
MR. DEMICHAEL: he wrote my records... in City Hall.

MR. HODES: And Frank Holstein is turning off the mike. Now, Frank Holstein is standing on the -- where you can't -- the audience can't see you, but he's at the bandstand behind the curtain, like, where the band can see him. And he's kneeling down and he's calling with his little finger to Brunis to get away from the piano and Brunis isn't getting away. He's doing ten, 15 minutes.

Now, this is the scene. We got everything facing us. Now the next deal, let's get Wild Bill. I call Wild Bill, he wants $275. I says to Brunis, in our meeting with the band, let's give it to him. I'll keep track of the books, you won't lose a dime. When we hit the road and start making money, he still gets $275 and we get more, and we build it up that we all get even.
'That son of a bitch ain't going to get a dime more than me, he ain't worth it.'
This is Brunis?
So, of course, there went that idea. And then the dickering -- and Fred Williamson discovered that I couldn't handle those guys, which was true.
Nobody could.

That's it. I found that nobody could handle them. They just were not going to be handled. And he must have had an idea about me, based on what happened in New York. But at that time, Brunis was not the Brunis that I met in Chicago. When I played (unintelligible) with Brunis, George was not that same George. In those next years, he had changed more or something.

And, really, -- so we blew it. We lasted 11 weeks. We were due to stay there six months. And we broke it. They had to let us go. And I looked around Chicago and I found that there was work, and there was a young fellow there that was
doing a lot for jazz. His father was a very wealthy man.
John Skenk?

John Skenk, with the money. John Skenk was interested in me putting a band together. And we had met at -- Chippy Hill left us and went to New York. And within weeks, she was dead, and they brought her back to New York, and I was the only white person at the funeral.
They brought her --
Brought her body back to be buried.
in New York?

No, in Chicago. And John Skenk was there and said, we got togetherness, and we wanted to book me and manage me. And we set that up. And I thought, well, looks to me that there could be work here. Freddie Williamson gave me two weeks in Minneapolis at a bar behind the bar. And the boss is running around for three days, moving the microphones while I'm playing.
And finally, it dawns on me. Who am I following? He says, Red Allen. I says, you can move mikes from now til Doomsday, you're never going to get me sounding like that band.
You were playing solo?
Solo, following the Red Allen band, the loudest jazz band I've ever heard.
Yeah.
For a small group. And I'm following him,

one man. So it didn't work out. Two weeks, I found out I couldn't do a single, there wasn't a jazz joint special. So I came back to Chicago and Skeak came up with a Rupneck's job, and here I am, involved in a jazz band. And again, it turned out to be all white, either Skeak's doing or -- I don't know. Chicago was not against me having a mixed band at the Blue Note. But, again, they told me, in Chicago you ask questions and go halfway.
And I know that Lee Collins, they were jamming with Lee Collins here and there. But there was still strictly white bands and black bands.

Yeah. Red Saunders, who was very close to the black union, said there was an understanding that black musicians could only work certain places in the Loop. Petillo's union - not that, but they didn't want mixed bands and they didn't want black musicians, black bands, playing too much in the Loop. And he and Harry Gray, the president of the black local, came to this disagreement.

And that of course killed my act at that time. And of course, that puts you at the mercy of the talent available. And usually, the talent available, there may be something wrong with it if it's very good. It's either they get too loaded or something, or they show up late. Because if they are very good, they're probably out of your reach, or they can go and get their own job. And this you find out.
So I did the best I could. And I stayed at Rup- neck's 18 months the first time.
Where was Rupneck's?

That was 5900 North Broadway on Thorndale, I think it was, right around the corner. And tremendous, we packed the joint. And I had Floyd O'Bryan and different trumpet players. I had little Muggsy Davis I had Jimmy Isle for awhile, different people.
A five-piece band.

No, we didn't have a bass player. I did have a black drummer and I can't think of his name. But he was more like a Mexican, and he'd worked with a band that made what they called race records at that time in Chicago, and they had a New Orleans trumpet player -- I can't think of his name.
That wasn't Booker T. playing drums, Booker T. Washington?
No, no, I can't think of his name. But, anyway, he worked in the post office, this guy. But, again, he used to really overdrink and I had to change that. But we lasted.

That was the job where Floyd O'Bryan sat at the bar and the boss bought us a drink, and the boss must have -- Floyd, 'were losing money. And Floyd looked at him and says, bullshit. Because talk like that was unheard of. That was the same boss that loved "Rampart Street Parade." That was his number. And anytime we bought a drink for the band, play
Rampart.
Who was he?

Frank Rupneck. Well, now, it just happened that in that period I was using two trumpet players. One would come in at 9:00 and play til 12:00, and one would come in at 12:30 and go till 3:00. It was a 9:00 to 3:00 job. Now, Frank bought the band a drink and the new trumpet player has gone up there. He hasn't played yet. We got to play Rampart.
Well, you know what happened to his lip? He just blew the number. And Frank cut us off from the bar, he says, don't give him anymore to drink.
And hadn't even --
And had nothing. He just walked in cold with a cold lip.
After the Blue Note gig and meeting Skank you decided to resettle in Chicago.

I figured I could work half as hard and accomplish as much, as far as making a livelihood. There seemed to be enough work here. And I still have family here. And I decided to try it, and sent for my family and tried to settle here, see what was here.
And I found out very quickly that there wasn't that much happening, but by that time we were settled, and we had to go on the road, too. We had to take this small band and sign
with William [agency] Morris and start going around. Toronto, Detroit, St. Louis, Denver. All over, playing a week here, a week there.

To get back to it, I was finding out that to keep a band, you had to go out on the road because there wasn't enough places in Chicago to play. R. U. neck's -- then Danny Alvin got the job at R. U. neck's or somebody else. Johnny Lane. There was a few leaders all fighting for the same work. And so about 1953, I ran out of work for bands. And that means I had to do something. So I went to work at Jazz Limited, which was a new experience.

There was a club that played music, no dancing. And they had started with people like Bechet, Sidney Bechet, and Big Sid Catlett and Joe Sullivan and Doc Evans. They've had some main people. And now they were down to just using one or two local names without importing. And salaries were -- well, you were getting a weekly stipend that's not great, but it's certainly scale or over.

And you were playing jazz music of a kind. I mean, it's not what you would choose to play all the time. Occasionally you'd get to play some you would choose to play. And the tempos are not what you would choose to play. It's the leader, the leader sets the style and the leader owns the club. So you go along, if you want the job.
And I needed the job. So I stayed there for quite a few months and then I remember how I lost the job. I didn't

lose it because I caused any problems. I lost it because the leader went on vacation, and during the two weeks that he was gone the business improved, and I was running the band. I had no salary, but --
No extra.

No extra, but just to run the band. But business improved. It did much better, for whatever reason. And when he came back, I saw him sit down at the table during intermission, and he was holding his fist to his head and thinking and thinking. And I was wondering, what is he thinking?

What he was thinking was, he was looking at the band and he didn't see the band, he saw chairs. And he looked at that piano chair and saw that he could save money on that chair. He was paying that chair too much. He could pay it a little less.

And he called me over and says, Art, he says, I don't want you to think I don't appreciate what you did while I was gone. But I'm going to have to give you your notice. And I went home and told my wife, you know, we can't stand too much appreciation. I was out of work.

So, back again, to get a band because you have to eat, you've got to work. And there's no solo places in Chicago in the '50s. To play solo, you have to sing, you have to tell jokes. You have to come on with the come-on. I hadn't arrived to where I could talk to audiences anyway. And certainly,

drinking audiences kind of -- I don't know how to handle them too well. Some people know. I've seen one guy turn to the audience, one trumpet player and say to somebody who was getting obnoxious, he says, I don't come on your job and take your broom and shovel away.

And you develop remarks like that, and I wasn't into that. So I decided I better think of something else, the single was out. There was no place where you could play as a single for people to come in and just listen to you. There was no place. I don't know if there's anyplace in Chicago now, that they would pay to hear a single play by himself. And this is the tragedy.

So I have to go get a small band because they will pay for a small band, and maybe get a vocal in there and some sort of entertainment. And this is what I'm doing continuously. And with ups and downs. And meanwhile, I get a date from Mercury, the Hot Fivers, they gave me that date. And that's through an agent, again. He was able to maneuver a date. And this is -- it gives you a little picture of what the music business is like.

One of the tunes I decided to record, of course, is 'Grandpa Spells.' And I think the A&R man was David something, I'm not sure. But he was also a pianist, had his own band. Anyway, I recorded this record and 'Sweet Georgia Brown' and other things. And for those times -- and it still is a good
record, for what it started out to be. It's concise, it's more like a John Kirby band.
Is that Art Hodes and his High Fivers?
High Fivers.
High Fivers.

And for what it started out to do, it was tight and crisp, and I wouldn't call it traditional jazz and the purists probably didn't like it. But there was a lot of people that liked it and bought it. And the record don't come out. We wait month after month after month and it's still ain't out.

Now I go up to Minneapolis to play a date, and somebody says, hey, you play 'Grandpa's Spells', I just heard it by Liberace. And then I get back to Chicago and the band leader, the A&R man, has put out a record. What they did was, they heard me do 'Grandpa's Spells', and they loved the material. So somebody got Liberace to do it. Then their A&R man did it, then after they milked it, then they put out my record.

I found this is the business music, as opposed to the business of playing music. This is the business music. And most musicians don't care for the business of music, and you can see why. There's a thing I never heard of. I'm now a talent scout. If they had paid me for bringing them that tune, it would have been a different thing. Say, here, you brought us
a tune and we want him to do it first because he's got a bigger name, and he's money. They didn't say that, they just held me up.

But nine months later, I was grateful that I had a date, because nobody around town was getting dates. Chicago is not a place to record, if you had a band. It's not a place now to record, as anyone knows, you have to find an angel somewhere. Big companies won't do it. I went up to Mercury after I made "Plain Old Blues", and DownBeat -- it was just fortunate at that month they reviewed the record, it was the only record that got five stars. Because of that, the policy was to buy 250 records, I believe, and give them away with subscriptions.
Yeah, with -- right.

And that record sold better, I was told, than any of that series that they put out. And I heard -- and I'm not sure it's the truth, but I heard that it had sold as many as 27,000. And I thought, man, that's -- I ought to get a date. And I went up there, and whoever I talked to said, that ain't enough for us.
Jack Tracy had left by --
He'd left. He says, you've got to have at least 100,000 for us to be interested. That'll start making us money.
Sounds like Green, who became President.
And so I didn't get a date. Now, for a

little company, I found out, if I would be ever fortunate enough to sell 2,700 records, they would be in seventh heaven. So the thing I discovered was to record for small labels, as other musicians have discovered, because they will keep you alive, they don't expect that much, they're not in that big business, and you have a voice. Suddenly, you have something to say, it's said.

And so I discovered this about the recording business. But we had all sorts of experiences of going up to the agency and asking me again, what else do you do, we know you play, but what else? I have a friend who's got a vice president of NBC, he's a tremendous friend of him, he owes him a favor. And this guy is a real good friend of mine.
(End of Side One.)

T2 52 Ya bum, you shouldn't be out of work, I'll meet you tomorrow and drive you to the city. We'll go up to NBC, go up to NBC, man comes out of conference and talks to us. He is a friend of my friend. He says to me, Art, what can you do with your five men that I couldn't pull five men out of the 95 that Petrillo says I've got to have, and approximate what you're doing? If not do the same thing.

Honestly, I can't say no to that. He says, now, why should I go buy five more men, when I'm fortunate to have 95? So this was the other side of the thing. The union was making some musicians a lot of work and a lot of money. The few were
getting it all, the many, scraping for what was left on the bottom.
The same story.
Same story. So this was the Chicago scene that I was involved in. And -- which brings me to the time I finally looked at my hands and said, what am I doing, and I started teaching.

And then work, whatever I could and then what saved me was in 1959, Bob Scobey came to town and called me. Now, I had bad recollections of Scobey from the Lou Waters band. So when he called me, I was visiting my daughter. And I says, no, I don't read that good to read your charts. I'm not interested in joining a band. But he had Tut Soper, and Tut, again, had done something in the band that they wanted him to leave yesterday, for some reason. I don't know what he did. I don't blame it on his playing because I always thought, if he wanted to, he could play like Earl Hines, on that style.
He can play more like Earl Hines than Earl Hines can. ... piano player I ever played with.

Yeah. I thought he could be excellent, yeah. So they wanted to get rid of him right away, that night. So Bob just brushed away every one of my remarks. Says, you don't have to look at the music, just sit at the piano and if you know the tune, play it. If you don't know it, lay out. You don't have to do nothing, just show up, please.
I couldn't say no. So I came. It's the luckiest thing I ever did. I went there and I played, the arrangements I could read I read.
This was on Bourbon Street?
This was on -- not Bourbon Street, but the other one, runs alongside. The Continental was the first job.
Oh, the Continental, yes, right.
I can't remember the street.
Walton.
Walton. Playboy magazine started somewhere in this street, because the guy came in and sat with us.
Yeah, he opened their first Playboy club there.

So that's the time, and I worked four days with the band, and made the record, 'Rampin' and Stompin'" Victor with them. I was very impressed with the band. Dave Black on drums, Rich Madison playing tuba, I think Beebee and that tall clarinet player on the West Coast, can't think of his name. He was with the band at that time. And, [Hicks] Huges of course, Clancy was playing banjo, and just had a -- they did an hour and 15 minute show that knocked me out.
And then they had this Toni Scott who later got famous and got out of reach for which I was very grateful.
Toni Scott?
She sang.
Not the clarinet player.
No, that one-legged gal.
Oh, yeah, yeah.

Yeah, she became a purist -- modernist after she got discovered. This music was not her bag. She was now into 'Little Boy Blue' or something, I forgot. These tunes that the modernists -- if you sing them, you're hip. She got into that.

Anyway, at that time she was very normal and anxious for me to know her stuff. And went over it with her and everything. Four days, I fitted right in the band. But I told them I didn't want to stay, because I says, I can't join you because you're going to get up and move. And I'm not travelling that much. I had three offers from Louis Armstrong to join him.

And I have to think that I have Barney Bigard to thank for it. And the band -- whoever -- Frenchie, Frenchie looked at me and says, you belong in that scene. See, Earl had left, and before Joe Sullivan came in, they wanted me. And after Joe Sullivan came in they wanted me. So this is pre-Napoleon.
Marty Napoleon.
Martin Napoleon. This was pre-Marty --
I didn't know Joe had played with --
Yeah, he played there for awhile. And they wanted me in that, but I didn't want to travel. I decided,
if I go with him, then I no longer can decide my fate. I might not come back to Chicago for two years, and what am I going to do with my family? I got kids and everything. I can't do it.

So Scobie I couldn't do it, either. Scobie says, all right, how would you like to have your own band opposite me, a quartet? I says, fine, whatever money is fine. So I got Nappy Trotter, Buddy Smith, Earl Murphy, Art Hodes. Fine, great. Now, Nappy immediately gets a complex. He's got to go on after Scobie, in the band. So go out to the bar and get ready to play and all that, and got a show on.

Now, it was the easiest job in the world. All we had to do was play that intermission. Now, instead of letting it down so that the people could -- they had an hour and a quarter show. They were raised to the sky, here we come, the thundering herd. Like man, you know, to break it down. Buddy Smith is not going to be backstaged by Dave Black. It was a scene, you know? And Bob Scobie had meanwhile taken me aside and said, Art, can't you talk to those guys? It's not that -- I'm not worried about them cutting us or anything. It's just -- the room is so high, now you want to lower it. Just play for kicks, play the blues, play things like that. But don't come on like -- now, meanwhile, Earl Murphy and Buddy Smith are very thick. I had Buddy Smith at Ruppel's, after I came back, several times, in a trio. They were very thick.
Now, one night, something happened in the rhythm section, it fell apart or something. And Murphy walked up to

Buddy and he says, what happened to the rhythm? And Buddy says, don't worry about it. That was all that was said. And that was like waving a red flag. Murphy, he just couldn't understand how he could say, don't worry about it.

Now, as Buddy later explained it to me, it was something might have happened at that moment, forget it, it'll be all right the next moment. Murphy didn't take it that way, that he's not worrying about the rhythm. So they stopped talking. And they stopped talking -- Murphy didn't want to stand near him. And now the boss is looking at me because I got to put the bass in front of the piano. I'm the leader and the bass player is standing right in front of me so he can get away from the drummer. I can't explain to him that they're not talking to each other. I got all this B.S. going on, the price of having a band and being able to work.

And it was ridiculous and I couldn't cure it. Well, finally, the Continental -- Bob did leave for a stretch and they put Earl Hines in. And now, there's a story I want to tell about that. Earl Hines is coming in, we got to get a piano. They had an upright Kimball and it was a gas but now we got to get a grand for Earl, right? Spending $4100 a week on music, got to get a grand. Of course, that included the other gypsy band that was playing in the other room or something.
Okay. You know what that guy did? This genius who was running the club? He found that there was a piano at some

dray house or something that had been standing there for years. He could get it for $150. And he got that $150 piano and had it hauled and tuned and painted black. And I know it was painted black because I followed Earl and the paint came off on my shirt. For a long time I couldn't get rid of it. The paint was still fresh.
And it was a dog. What could you buy for $150? I couldn't get over it. Here's a man spending $4100 on music, and he's going to give the star a $150 piano.
A wet, salvaged piano.
And this is the thinking, the typical thinking of bosses. Another story was working the Sahara. And the boss is sitting at the bar with a girl. And I heard that story.

Now, he was at least an aware boss about this music. This is the story I got. He asked this the waitress girl, 'what's wrong with the business?' She says, 'don't you know? It's the band.' The band gets fired. It's another old story. The guy goes next door to the band that's doing business, he says, 'how you guys doing?' 'Oh, man, we're doing all right.' 'I'm not doing so good.' 'Well, why don't you change the band?' First thing, change the band.
So I'm running into this change-the-band, work two weeks, work a week. If the cash register don't ring, the boss is not interested in the music that he's going to stick out,

And it's just a bad scene and we've got to put in seven hours. So, 9:00 to 4:00, we drive back to that same restaurant and he buys me a hamburger and he pays me a Class Z scale. After he's taken out Social Security. I got something like $17.15. And I'm not going to get -- and I've got to pay my fare both ways. And I'm not going to get home til about 7:00 in the morning. I says to him, 'do me a favor.' He says, what? I says, 'you know, you got my name on a piece of paper? Take it and tear it up. I can't afford to know you. Tear it up. Don't call me, just tear it up.'

And that was it. I never worked for him again, he never called me or nothing, which saved me. But this is another scene that I would run into with these kind of jobbing things. But little by little, people got to know, not the musicians, especially, or the owners, but lay people got to know that I was available. And if they had a wedding on a Saturday, they could get me. They didn't have to worry because I'd be available.

So I was beginning to get these club dates. And between that and the teaching, -- it wasn't great, but we were beginning to get by, without working -- where I was going to get pushed out of work. And pretty soon, the Showboat Sahara, -- the Sorry S, or as the musicians called it, the Sorry Ass, got to be the last one I worked, just about. And of course, along about this time, I did an article for the Daily News,

'Tell It Like It Is.' And so I met Mr. Keegan or Hogan or -- and I asked him if he could open a door for me on television. See, I tried radio and Studs tried for me, but for me to do a program on radio, no, there's no place for me, unless you go out and get a sponsor.

So I couldn't do that, so I had to give up. I'm not capable of getting sponsors. So I tried to break the door down, and he says, well, maybe I could do something for you on Channel 11, WTTW. It was on on the South Side at that time. I went out there, and I auditioned. I played along and told the story of jazz as I knew it.

See, by that time I had done -- I had met a man who booked high schools in Wisconsin. And I did 88 schools in the dead of winter, 14 to 28 degrees that winter of '64. Had to get up like 3:00 in the morning and make sure your car ran, because at 6:00 you've got to get up, you've got to be at that school at 8:00. That's your first appearance. Two and three schools a day, that's $500 a week, paid very well. You paid your room, you paid your car, you paid all of it. And probably did 14 a week, two a day, or equivalent. You didn't work Sunday.

And -- the Wisconsin Bureau of Lectures. And I'd done that, and I developed a thing that I could do for kids, because you had to get out there for 25 to 45 minutes and the kids can be very rude at the high school age, or any age. You
have to come on, you have to prove yourself, you have to do something that gets through to them, or else they'll laugh at you.

For example, I used to have a line. I played Basin Street Blues. I changed all this, and I'd say, the opening line is, 'won't you come along with me,' or 'aren't you glad you came with me.' I used that all the time, til one 11-year-old boy in an audience of 1,000 -- I could hear him clear as a bell, say, 'I'm not.'
You know, that taught me never to ask questions, never to invite -- another time they told me, there was a kid --
A little audience participation.

They told me there was a kid that played good boogie wogie piano in the school, and I asked them, well, bring him out. Never did that again, because he was about 17 and he was full of hellfire. And he played up a storm, and what he could do, he could do.
And I said, now --
(Recording interrupted.)
And I developed this thing on jazz. Now, I'd done concerts at colleges. I'd been to Smith College, been to Connecticut College, I've been to any number of colleges in the East, talked on jazz.
Yeah, you've built up that circuit.
I've done that. I did it in New York.

I discovered that I could find a man and I paid for publicity. I've done all the things. New York taught me a lot. But I -- and I'd learn how to do it without records. The first time I did it at a college, it was State College, which is a Pennsylvania college.
Penn State.

Penn State. And in order to get there, I had to sleep in a neighboring town after working that night. I had to stay in a neighboring town, I couldn't sleep hardly at all. Catch a bus like 7:00 in the morning and be there at the school at 9:00.
And that place is in the middle of nowhere, in University Park.

And I was tired, I was in bad shape. And I got these records. I'm using records to talk about jazz, and then the piano. This is how you learn. And I put the record on, and it was a wind-me-up Victrola. It wasn't a plug-in. And I wound it up tight, at least, I thought I did. And I put on a Jelly Roll Morton record, which -- 500 boys in the room. They never heard Jelly Roll.

And it starts (singing). The record runs down, the machine runs down. And did you ever appear in front of an audience with 500 lads, you achieve laughter? They break up. Did you ever hear 500 people laughing while you're on stage, and you get red, blue, pink and azure? That's the last time I

used a record machine. They taught me very fast. I said to them, I think I better play the piano. And somebody says, I think you better. I went up and played and played and played, and when I got through, that house came down. I just played til the house came down. I just gave them my all and I just proved it.

But I knew that I could do it with playing. But I still hadn't had it all together. Like, these schools got it all together for me. I even played for high school kids. In many halls, you're sitting with -- the back of your head is facing them, 200 kids all around you. And you can feel a tomato flying through the air. And -- boom. But it never happened, and I built this little thing on jazz, and I brought it to WTTW, and did it and they liked it, but they couldn't give me no money. I says, I don't work for free. So I'll see you.
Maybe we should explain that WTTW is an educational --

Is an educational station. They didn't have the money. So I says, that's okay, could I have the tape? Says, oh, sure. Guy was very friendly, still one of my best friends, Bob Kaiser. So it wasn't his doing, they just didn't have the money. They gave me the tapes, I took them home.
And it was about a year later, they found enough money to pay me what the union scale was to do it. So I came back and did it again. And then they got interested in me
doing it with a band. And they had this guy, Rubenstein, Marty Rubenstein, kind of interviewing me and talking to me, the new and the old.
Yeah, he's a very fine pianist, too.

Yeah, very fine. And he sat and talked to me about jazz and we played, and I had Brunis and the regular guys. And that we got paid -- everybody got paid something and it was shown, wow. So then the station moved to 5200 North from the South, and time passed, and again, the opportunity came to us to do a show, alone.

I went up there and I did a show and I called it Plain Old Blues. That time, I had already recorded Plain Old Blues. Again, I sat down and talked about that it all started with a beat and I made a beat and I says, now the beat appeared "A Closer Walk with.." in spirituals and I played -- it appeared in church, it appeared on the railroad tracks when they were working, it appeared all over. But with the blues appeared everywhere. But always, that beat was there. And if it hasn't that got beat, it hasn't got it.

And I talked and played more, just small remarks. That show got an Emmy, a Chicago Emmy. And there was 13 shows -- 17 shows chosen for a Chicago Emmy and only two from a non-commercial station. "Book Beat" was one and this was the other. So that opened the door for them to do more things and get management to come up with some money.

So then we started doing Chicago things, and using Chicago men to back guests. So I used different people that would play. And brought in Barney Bigard and Doc Evans before he died. Pee Wee Russell was on before he died, Jimmy McPartland Eddie Condon before he died, Bud Freeman, besides J. C. Higginbothom and Parenti and people like that.
What was the name of that series?

Jazz Alley. And it was shown all over the country. 205 stations showed it. Now, the worst show I did in my estimation was the one with Eddie Condon and Tony Parenti, Smokey Starr, -- you mentioned this drummer, plays with a press roll.
Monty Monchoy?
Monty Monchoy, J.C. Higginbothom and myself. And the reason it was so bad, in my estimation, was because the fellows were so tired. They had come -- some of them had come from New York.

Now, Smokey played his butt off, played beautifully. And Tony Parenti, in spite of the fact that he was tired, played. But J.C. hadn't been playing, leaning up against the piano, he was tired. And that trip, they came from work without sleep. And then the engineer or somebody at the station, made a mistake. After the rehearsal, they said, fellows, there will be a two-hour intermission.
So the drinkers went out and drank. And there's a

funny story about Eddie Condon I have to tell because he came back with his brother, and we were about ready to go on, and Eddie called me over and said to me, Art, can you talk to the director and see if I can't get my brother to sit on stage with us, because he don't hear so good.
(Laughter.)
That's right, you had a prop audience.

A prop audience and a small stage. And this was the stage where Pee Wee Russell discovered that the prop bartender looked like a real bartender and started beckoning to him to come over and bring a drink while we were taping, and some very funny things, George Brunis trying to do a Ted Lewis in his hat, Ted Lewis always tumbles his top hat off and catches it and takes a little bow. And George couldn't catch it. On and on and on. We had some funny scenes and some worthwhile things were recorded.

But I guess the show where Eddie was speechless, and I really wanted him to talk. That's really why I got him, because I wanted to get Eddie talking about his life or jazz, any observation. And had he not been in a cast, we could have got some of that. But as it was, the camera man should have got an Oscar for identifying him but missing him, just showing enough of him that it was Eddie Condon, but not showing him the way he looked because he was just out of it. He was just barely sitting there.
And that was the show New York City heard, and they got crazy about it. That was the one. That's the -- in my estimation the worst show. They heard it, called me up.
Do you think it's because you -- you got a lot of things going on now, it seems things are going fairly well. Do you see that coming from that TV series?
The TV series helped me, but times are changing.
You also got the Columbia Artist --

Columbia Artists caught me and brought me in New York because of the television series, they did. They brought me in New York because of that, and gave me the tours. And the tours put us on our feet financially. If I tell you what the stars were making, I don't want to say this because the sidemen weren't getting that, but they were getting more money than they could have gotten in a year of Sundays in Chicago.
And you played subscription --
Subscription concerts. So everybody was doing very well.
All over the country.
Yeah. And I wasn't spending my money, I had nothing to spend it on. So I was saving it, and the government didn't take it all away. They did leave me some. I discovered what paying taxes was.
(Laughter.)

I suddenly found out that I wasn't going to get anything back, I was going to give them more. But it was a good feeling. All this came through these TV shows, admittedly so. But there was also movement. Jazz was becoming more -- there was an audience growing up and there was things going on in jazz all over the country. There was something in Colorado going on, there was something in Odessa, Texas, there was something in Decatur, there's something in Manassas. There are suddenly festivals.

And then the European scene opened up. And all this helped make for more work for a select few musicians. Like our friend Kenny Davern says, five percent of the musicians in the country are making a livelihood out of music. Now, take that five percent and figure out how many of them are jazz musicians. And you will find that in New York City, if you find 50 you've found quite a few that are making it strictly playing jazz. And in Chicago, two, three, one, four, how many? Playing jazz. I'm not thinking about --
Nothing but jazz?
Yeah, I'm not thinking about the fellow that appears in the studio --
Well, some guys are doing nothing but playing jazz but they're not doing too well.
This is what I -- yeah. It's a hanging-
on thing, you're just making enough paper. So this is the story. But it -- still, it's gotten better for a few.
Well, it got better for you. With the tours of Europe as a single.
Right, right.
I mean, the recognition --

Is coming, much better. There's a new age, they don't want to know nothing about what somebody said about anybody. And I've always said, if you can get by the agents and the critics and get to the people, you're home free. I found out doing the concerts that there's thousands and thousands, hundreds of thousands of people that would love the music, if they could hear it.
The point is, how can you get it to them to hear it? That's the whole point. We're not up against the people listening. We're up against the person in-between.
Up against the music business.

Yeah, that's right. Who's the guy that writes about you? Who's the guy that books you? How do you find out, when you're talking to a booker who was a violin player, never liked jazz, couldn't stand it? Do you think he's going to plug it? No, man, I'm going to plug rock 'n roll, because that's where the money is. Art, I'm sorry, I like you as a person, there's nothing in the world I won't do for you. And unfortunately, there's nothing I can do for you. I'll do

nothing. And this gets to be a big laugh. So you do it for yourself, to the best of your ability. But as you say, it's gotten better. You can play a festival. You can go occasionally to Europe. You get lucky, you do something friendly like you did for Harriet Choice of the Tribune. In return, she turns out and talks to George Wein, you've got to get him one time. So George Wein, who is not an Art Hodes fan, by any stretch of the imagination, gets me because there's some opening he has to fill.

I get to Europe because of him. And there's two fellows that are booking singles that hear me. That's the sequence of events. So they heard me and they says, hey, man, will you come over for me? So that means three weeks working in Europe, three and a half. There's a man in England that won't book me, unfortunately. Now, he's booking all these other people, but to tell you the truth, he won't pay me what I can get going to Germany for this other man. He just -- I don't know what, in Europe he says, England is a poor country. I don't know what they're getting paid, I really don't. But it takes a certain amount. You set a standard. You say I want so much money. And if you don't get it, you don't say to a man, what will you give me? When you start that kind of nonsense, you're lost.
So you set a standard. You lose some and you win some, is the way I figure it. I've just set a standard. I'm

not higher -- I've talked to different musicians, and I know I'm not getting what Joe Venuti or Red Norvo would have gotten. But I'm getting what I think is a fair sum to bring me over there. I'm not living in the same house I have, I have to live in a room where there's just a shower and no bathtub, or some -- things like that. There's no place to eat in the room. After work, everything is closed.
Just like Annapolis.

Yeah, this is what I mean. There are sacrifices and you should get paid for it, if you're going to do this. And so some places you win, and some places you fail. Then you run into this other thing. You're the wrong color. Somebody says, you can't come to France to play blues because you're the wrong color. And I see some -- if I use the word bum, I mean musical bum, who's the right color but he can't play blues. He's hardly playing, and he's getting over quite often. And you wonder. That's the other side of it.

It's all part of the picture. You don't get bitter about it. It's just one of those things. People -- and the final analysis, what you're up against is ignorance. I mean, if you didn't have ignorance --
In everything.
In everything. If people were hip to what jazz was, jazz wouldn't be struggling. The kids would get to hear it. Why isn't it that a kid cannot turn on his radio and
hear Art Tatum playing, I Would Do Most Anything For You, or Fats Waller playing?

Because they've got to sell those records to those kids. The leading problem with the music business is that the big money in the music business is controlled by record companies and they are the taste makers and that's why jazz is -- that's not why jazz is more popular than it was a few years ago, but it's certainly why jazz is not paying much more than it was a few years ago.

Yes, and none of these -- there's very few people that will do something for the sake of educating people and uplifting them, and you find that in music especially. And that's why when you turn on your radio, it's an arid desert. There's nothing. You can search that radio. Maybe if you're on New York City or something, or maybe if you're around Chicago, possibly. Or maybe New Orleans. But for the most part, nothing. You don't hear this. And a kid coming up in college, anywhere, there's no jazz library on the air that they can say, well, I'll tune in for a half hour. Today, they got Fats, they got this, they got that, they got the best thing going. It's happenstance. If you do catch it, it's happenstance.
It's not going out all the time. So for that reason, the jazz man has an uphill battle to fight, because what kind of music is that? You can't play 'Leroy Brown' -- now, I'm going

far back, you can see how far back I'm reaching, when I mention Leroy Brown, which is not a bad -- but they're doing things that we're not into. We got rock, hard rock, bubble gum rock. It's gone out of our reach. And we're not against it, we're up against it. If they could just hear what we have, and then make a choice.
In summary, if you had it to do all over again, --

I'm not going to say I'd do it all over you, like the joke. No, if I had to do it all over again, I'd consider myself one of the most fortunate people in the world that the direction that I took, that I stayed out of big bands, where I would have been -- I could learn how to play in big bands, it's not that difficult. I went for extra schooling one time for four years, practiced four hours a night, four to eight hours. I could have gone for whatever I needed and get it, if my interest was there.

But, oh, I made a lot of mistakes. It's ridiculous to say I would do it the same way. But basically, the way I followed the music, oh, there's no question about it. I'm sorry I didn't come in a little earlier, so I could have hung around with Joe Oliver. I missed some people. Just like, from where you sit or the next person sits, he wished he could come in ten years earlier because he missed some people. And he hated to have missed.

But when I came in, it was still the golden age of, not only jazz, but entertainment. We had Clayton Jackson Durrant. How many people caught an act in person? I did. And -- I mean, who are around. And I've become an antique. Look, he's still breathing. But I can --
The radio came in; talkies - movies.

I've heard these people and I saw them in person, and this was a great thing, because today, it's a tinsel thing. The -- I don't say that the kids don't have the talent. They don't have a chance to develop it, hardly. You know how many people have said what I am saying about fighters, they have no fight clubs where they can develop? They go from amateurs right into the ring, the Madison Square Gardens? Comedians say they have no small clubs to develop. Musicians have no small clubs where they pay their dues.
Well, society has changed. Same way with baseball games. No more minor league teams.

No, everything is -- and for that reason, we have lost something. We've lost this tremendous training that these people had and they became what they are. And it's not that these people today -- I'm not faulting them, I'm faulting the conditions. And you say, in summing up, would you do it over again? Do you call where I'm living today progress, when I have to worry if my kids are going to make it when they grow up, or is the water going to be poisoned, the woods are

going to be dead? Is this better than the horse and buggy? This is what they tried to convince us about our jazz. They says, our jazz went out with buckled shoes. [now] "It's the new thing." Well, is it the new thing in life that's that great? Tell me, is it the new thing? The dog-eat-dog, like you said about the record business? They don't care about anybody, just want to make money and all that?

I mean, I don't see that big progress. True, I stand astounded when I see the moon, and realize that man walked on it. I can't believe it, I can't visualize it. And I think that's great. But why can't we learn how to live? And so that is all part of the same thing. I'm delighted that I lived in that age and paid my dues and played that kind of music. I couldn't have gotten a better deal. The guys that came along, like Wingy Manone. Instead of going with Joe Schmo and his Hollywood Raspberries or his Society Bluebirds, which I could have gone with --
You could have made that turn.
Made that turn, I was into it. They wanted me. I was the one that screwed that up because my inclinations were the other side.
You followed your heart.
Right.
And you have no regrets.
Oh, how can you regret it? I mean, I

-- may I say this in closing? I met a pianist who worked during the same years that I did, in bars and clubs. And he read the specs and he played the floor show, and he saved his money and he lost his eyesight and he lost all his money in the Crash.

And what did he have to show for it? Because it wasn't enjoyable, it was a job that he went to work to get. And how many people do you read about that work so that they can retire and then drop dead a year later, after they've built that house? They have failed to live today, and this is what jazz music has given us. This they can't take away.
When you play that chorus, --
It's part of the moment.

And how can anybody put a price on it? What you get out of music is priceless. So when you say, would you have done it, I would have done it sooner and quicker and more avidly. I'd have put more of my life into it, if I could, so I could have gotten more of it. No question about it. I don't regret a dime I lost or the meals I missed. So what? Big deal. I ate at the House of Parliament, big deal, big deal.

The meaningful things in life to me are the real things. I do not stand in front of a French painting and say, isn't that wonderful, when I don't understand it. I look at it and say, I don't understand it. But I do understand that bowl

of cherries, I do understand the vase. This I understand. Now, if that's ignorance on my part, I admit ignorance. But I'm alive watching this. If I'm ignorant of all these scales and exercises, you guys are cutting up on the piano. I'm sorry, I'm ignorant. You ain't said nothing to me except that you've gone to school much more than I ever did. You learned a lot more about the instrument than I have learned. But you forgot one thing, you forgot where the sure-enough is.
Right. Thank you, Art.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
